entries.title: Boy, 13, critically wounded after being shot by 9-year-old in Fuller Park
entries.summary: <p>A 13-year-old boy is in critical condition after being shot by another child on Friday afternoon in Fuller Park.</p><p>Police said a 9-year-old boy was inside a home in the 5200 block of South Wells Street with a firearm. He reportedly fired one shot around 4 p.m. on Friday, hitting a 13-year-old boy in the shoulder. </p><p>The wounded boy was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was in critical condition. </p><p>A handgun was found at the scene, police said. Detectives are investigating the shooting. </p>

entries.title: Have you been swarmed by biting flies? Why they're 'no joke'
entries.summary: <p>From Rogers Park to Calumet Park, many people in the Chicago area are reporting a surge in flies.</p><h3><b>Are there more flies, especially ones that bite?</b></h3><p>The public health departments of Chicago and Illinois don’t track biting flies. But anecdotally, they seem ubiquitous. Social media is buzzing with people lamenting getting attacked by flies everywhere from Belmont Harbor to Logan Square.</p><p>“Today at a park in West Town I got swarmed by like seven flies after sitting on the ground for less than five minutes with my dog. Those bites are no joke,” wrote one Reddit user this week.</p><p>Another Reddit user had to leave Oak Street Beach, “because there were hundreds of flies that kept landing on me and staying on my skin. Felt like tiny needles. I’ve never experienced this at the beach.”</p><p>Lifeguards at lakefront beaches have been spotted wielding flyswatters and flies are swarming dogs on walks.</p><h3><b>Why are there more flies?</b></h3><p>Very wet and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>hot weather</u></a> in recent months could be a factor.</p><p>This summer, the Chicago area has seen some of the most <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/14/chicago-area-under-flood-watch-friday-night-through-saturday-morning" target="_blank" ><u>severe storms</u></a> in recent years. It has also been very hot, with several <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>heat waves</u></a>.</p><p>Wet and warm conditions are typically good for breeding insects. But Nina Salem, founder of the Insect Asylum in Avondale, said favorable weather conditions vary for different species.</p><p>Yet Salem noted that she and other wildlife rehabilitators have been seeing a big uptick of “fly strikes.” That’s when flies lay eggs on animals such as squirrels and raccoons. After hatching, flies burrow into animals, alive and dead.</p><p>Salem cautioned against washing any affected animals because water will trigger hatching of eggs, which look like white rice.<b> </b>If someone spots a fly strike on wildlife, they should contact a permitted wildlife rehabilitator for assistance, Salem said.</p><h3><b>What kind of flies are we likely seeing? </b></h3><p>There are many kinds of biting flies, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/environmental-health-protection/structural-pest-control/biting-flies.html" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois Department of Public Health</u></a>.</p><p>But the stable fly is a likely culprit because it peaks in late summer and early fall. It’s gray with four dark stripes behind the head. This bloodsucker “will fly several miles to bite livestock (hence the name), pets and people,” said the health department’s website. “They typically bite in early morning or late afternoon and often attack the ankles, inflicting a sharp, stabbing pain.”</p><p>Stable fly larvae “live in and eat decaying vegetation that washes up along the shore,” according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nps.gov/piro/planyourvisit/insects.htm?fbclid=IwY2xjawUH3qlwZG9mBWV4dG4DYWVtAjEwAGJyaWQRMU1Cc3llYmI1eGNSOFQ3emFzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEerYLCiCHpRQ5C5qu-N1XnczRjkAZrZMpzyKDbxDnXIYz7WX-6-70vb1_TQ44_aem_mJvCRaold8J2_yP2tIggBQ" target="_blank" ><u>National Park Service</u></a> in Michigan’s Pictured Rocks. They don’t transmit disease to humans, but “are annoying enough to drive people away from beaches.”</p><p>Stable fly outbreaks have occurred along the shores of Lake Michigan, Chris Stone, medical entomologist at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, wrote in an email. “This species is considered to be more abundant in years with high rainfall. So a peak this year would make some sense,” he said.</p><p>Other biting flies include deer flies, which are most abundant in the spring, as well as horse flies. Some horse flies are entirely black, while “greenheads” are light brown with shiny green eyes. Larvae live in water or moist locations.</p><h3><b>Are fly bites especially painful?</b></h3><p>They can be.</p><p>Stable flies suck blood through a pointed proboscis. “They have bayonetlike mouthparts with rasping teeth at the tip that they use to cut through or abrade the skin to create a pool of blood on which they feed,” Stone explained.</p><p>Deer and horse flies bite with “scissor-like mouthparts that cut into skin, causing blood flow which the flies lap up,” according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. This crude blood sucking can be especially painful.</p><h3><b>What are officials doing about the flies?</b></h3><p>Chicago Park District “has not received an influx of concerns regarding the presence of biting flies, mosquitos and other insects in our parks,” Michele Lemons, director of communications, wrote in an email.</p><p>The park district said it hasn’t seen park use drop.</p><p>“In fact, for many of our programs, we saw an increase in participation this summer,” said Lemons.</p><p>But on Friday morning, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/lfparksandrec?__cft__[0]=AZhDcdSG8DeQ6phyV_TZEX8t66jpYq1JKPBzz_-N-mvwmc2g7KbOPwA0TYWTBM-M9NVnOut-x9HMsHc8BbjWvBXmRcGHbJ7A_QJfkzbq4n16kHOFBaQYhcb06UspnnduhB8NvHSqYvH_9Cpo0CmJoks4vQ8eZ2xq&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R" target="_blank" >Lake Forest Parks and Recreation</a> department treated Forest Park Beach with an “EPA-approved product.”</p><p>The department said on <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/lfparksandrec/posts/pfbid06SgbUA59sH1CXtqtmn5piYeZGFUKFY3JzFmKvpURdU9qPTsFBvDM7nz6tjgZQwmVl" target="_blank" ><u>Facebook</u></a>, “While we can all agree our beach is amazing, the latest increase in fly activity is not!”</p><p>Indiana Dunes National Park warned about an outbreak of biting flies on Facebook, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.audacy.com/wbbm780/news/local/biting-flies-are-swarming-indiana-dunes-beachgoers" target="_blank" >WBBM News Radio</a> in Indiana. Park staff noticed a surge in biting flies on some eastern beaches about a week ago. </p><p>On Thursday, the Illinois Department of Public Health said it’s working on updating guidelines on managing flies and bites.</p><h3><b>What can I do?</b></h3><p>Most insect repellent doesn’t work on stable flies. Since they target legs and ankles, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nps.gov/piro/planyourvisit/insects.htm?fbclid=IwY2xjawUH3qlwZG9mBWV4dG4DYWVtAjEwAGJyaWQRMU1Cc3llYmI1eGNSOFQ3emFzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEerYLCiCHpRQ5C5qu-N1XnczRjkAZrZMpzyKDbxDnXIYz7WX-6-70vb1_TQ44_aem_mJvCRaold8J2_yP2tIggBQ" target="_blank" ><u>National Park Service</u></a> recommended wearing long pants and socks — not ideal for the beach.</p><p>In any case, stable flies can pierce through clothing, according to fly control company <a class="Link" href="https://info.spalding-labs.com/biting-stable-flies/" target="_blank" ><u>Spalding Labs</u></a>.</p><p>Salem noted that parasitic wasps can eat flies. But if fly predators aren’t handy, she and Stone suggested treating clothes with permethrin, a chemical insecticide.</p><h3><b>How long will this last?</b></h3><p>A stable fly’s <a class="Link" href="https://extension.okstate.edu/programs/livestock-entomology/stable-flies" target="_blank" ><u>lifespan</u></a> is 20 to 30 days. In the U.S., their peak season is July through September. But they can remain into October in warmer regions.</p><p>This summer, the Chicago area has endured heat waves, tornadoes, rainstorms, wildfire smoke and deafening <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/cicadas-louder-mating-brood-decibels-coping-mechanisms-dog-days-summer-heat-trees" target="_blank" ><u>cicada</u></a> choruses. Now it’s biting flies. What’s next?<br></p>

entries.title: Chicago sports’ bright future on display as Bears, Bulls, Cubs stars have ‘started something pretty cool’
entries.summary: <p>“Chicago’s got a lot to look forward to.”</p><p><b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> couldn’t have said it any better after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/03/pete-crow-armstrong-nl-player-of-the-month-august-alex-bregman-stats-kevin-gausman-brewers" >his latest MVP moment</a>, one that came in front of his fellow Chicago sports icons-in-the-making.</p><p>The Cubs’ center fielder smashed a victory-defining homer in the thick of a pennant race, giving Wrigleyville another reason to go nuts.</p><p>But with Bears quarterback <b>Caleb Williams</b> and Bulls youngsters <b>Matas Buzelis</b> and <b>Caleb Wilson</b> taking in the game from behind the Cubs’ dugout, that revelry expanded to fans of all stripes across the city.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">are they really your friends if they don't ride for you like this? <a href="https://t.co/wEHBxNIEho">pic.twitter.com/wEHBxNIEho</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2095684452877750511?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 4, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>It illuminated the potential of what could be coming: these guys causing celebrations for a generation of Chicago sports fans.</p><p>“I thought last night, for Chicago sports fans — or if you were at Wrigley last night — was really special,” Cubs manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said Friday. “They’ve started something pretty cool, for sure.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/03/bears-caleb-williams-hot-ones-debut-top-5-moments-ben-johnson-quarterback-nfl-hot-wings" >Friends of Crow-Armstrong</a>, the trio got massive cheers when shown on the video board, with the camera panning to Crow-Armstrong in the dugout, who pointed right back at them.</p><p>“Those are good people, those are my people,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Those are great representatives of Chicago.”</p><p>It was a rarity, this city-wide star power under one roof. How often do the complex schedules of football, basketball and baseball even allow for such a moment?</p><p>Williams is already one of the higher-profile quarterbacks in the NFL after leading the Bears to a string of unbelievable comeback victories last season, including over the rival Packers in the playoffs.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong has been on the sidelines at Soldier Field before. He hopes to be there again.</p><p>“Would I like to see the Packers get swept this year? Absolutely,” Crow-Armstrong said, knowing his audience. “I’m excited to go to all those games and show up just like he has.”</p><p>As the Bulls look toward a future they hope is brighter than what’s played out in recent seasons, they’re looking at Buzelis and Wilson – first-round picks in two of the last three years – as exciting cornerstones.</p><p>Sure, there was no representation from the Blackhawks on Thursday, but <b>Connor Bedard</b> is a player worth being equally excited about.</p><p>And while the White Sox, with playoff dreams of their own, and Cubs are rarely counted as allies, there’s more commonality there than you might think.</p><p>“It’s good for people to play into that and believe in that rivalry,” Crow-Armstrong said. “But at the same time, for us, it’s such a good opportunity to showcase what the city has to offer athletically and on the baseball field, specifically.”</p><p>In other words, these are exciting times.</p><p>And there was no better visual encapsulation of that excitement than Thursday’s cross-sport get together.</p><p>“It’s huge having guys show up and support each other,” Crow-Armstrong said. “The friendship alone is great, and I’m lucky to have that. But to be able to show the city that we’re all pulling for each other and we all believe in each other is huge.”</p><h3><b>Shota stops mini skid</b></h3><p>Lefty starter <b>Shota Imanaga</b> responded to back-to-back clunkers with a strong outing Friday, throwing six innings of one-run ball against the Marlins.</p><p>Imanaga <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/23/cubs-mariners-brewers-nl-central-standings-shota-imanaga-stats-starting-rotation-playoffs" >made the shortest start of his career</a> two weekends ago against the Mariners, then gave up three homers in a loss to the Reds, ballooning his season total to a league-worst 33.</p><p>Friday, Imanaga stopped a streak of six straight starts with at least one homer allowed.</p><h3><b>Do-it-all PCA</b></h3><p>After his power display Thursday, Crow-Armstrong flashed his other abilities Friday, walking for the 74th time, stealing his 33rd base of the season, scoring on a wild pitch and making an eye-popping leaping catch against the center-field wall.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div entries.title: Legislative inspector general has some explaining to do
entries.summary: <p>In the past week or so, three women have told stories about their dissatisfaction with the way they were treated by the state’s legislative inspector general. And it’s clear that at least three of the four legislative leaders are quickly becoming fed up with the legislative inspector general and that another leader may have trouble sustaining his claim that one of his members was cleared of wrongdoing.</p><p>You may have seen the Chicago Tribune story about an unnamed female lobbyist who formally objected to the way she was treated by Legislative Inspector General Michael McCuskey during his sexual harassment probe of now-former Rep. Harry Benton, D-Plainfield. The lobbyist sent a letter to the four legislative leaders at the end of July claiming McCuskey had “violated the confidence of other victims and me, broke standard investigative norms, and made inappropriate comments” to her. </p><p>“Specifically,” she wrote, McCuskey “shared the names of the other victims and other confidential information about their cases with me without prompting, among other inappropriate statements and missteps.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ec0000" name="module-ec0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>The day after that story was published, my associate Isabel Miller reached out to Laura Jackson, who claimed she was sexually harassed by Rep. Amy “Murri” Briel, D-Ottawa, and made other allegations, including how drugs were provided to campaign workers. </p><p>Jackson worked on Briel’s 2024 campaign and then served as Briel’s deputy chief of staff. McCuskey ruled that her allegations were “unfounded” and Briel said the ruling proved everything Jackson said was false and the House Democrats began unapologetically ramping up support for Briel in her second race against Republican Liz Bishop.</p><p>Jackson told Isabel that she, too, had experienced some of the same McCuskey behavior as the unnamed lobbyist. McCuskey, she said, “shared other stories from other people and their experiences with [Briel].” Jackson also said McCuskey claimed Briel was “crazy.” Asked about that, Jackson insisted that McCuskey “verbatim called [Briel] ‘crazy’ and … was telling me about the things that they were saying on their side in the interviews, but he definitely called her crazy to me.”</p><p>Jackson said McCuskey’s stories were “very validating in a sense because it was like he was telling me, ‘Here's all these other shared experiences. Don't worry.’</p><p>“I don't remember if he did tell me names [of other accusers],” Jackson said. “He spoke about, I think it was like an environmental lobbyist group that had a lot of issues with her, and he told me about that. He shared with me about a story I had already known … about Briel yelling at one of (JB) Pritzker's staff openly, and just like berating him openly, but I don't think he told me that staff's name.”</p><p>We reached out to all four legislative leaders and showed them Jackson’s quotes. Three responded.</p><p>I asked Senate President Don Harmon’s spokesperson whether the Briel legislative inspector general investigation should be revisited. </p><p>The response: “Central to our ethics laws is that victims and witnesses know they will be treated with respect, confidentiality and professionalism in this process. We would encourage the Legislative Ethics Commission to take the appropriate steps to uphold those standards.”</p><p>The Legislative Ethics Commission is empowered by state law to request further investigation of a case by the legislative inspector general. The commission, which is equally divided between the two parties, also has the power to request an investigation by the Illinois attorney general.</p><p>Asked the same question about whether the Briel legislative inspector general investigation should be revisited, House Minority Leader Tony McCombie’s spokesperson issued a one-word response: “Yes.”</p><p>Senate Minority Leader John Curran also weighed in: “Yes, the LEC should reopen the investigation and ensure that all appropriate steps were taken, including referring any criminal activity to the appropriate law enforcement agency.”</p><p>House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch office did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>As a matter of policy, the legislative inspector general does not respond to news media inquiries about specific details of cases.</p><p>And then yet another woman who filed a detailed sexual harassment complaint against a different House Democrat a few years ago sent us a statement corroborating many of the complaints against McCuskey, who also deemed her allegations “unfounded.”</p><p>“His treatment of victims is unacceptable,” she wrote. “The LIG kept telling me he was a federal judge, and that I made him look incompetent and questioned his integrity of investigating. … If someone really comes forward with a serious sexual assault or a big case, nobody should have to talk to him.”</p><p>The Legislature needs to get to the bottom of this.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a00000" name="module-a00000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: After recent beluga deaths, Shedd Aquarium monitoring others for 'clinical concerns'
entries.summary: <p>Days after two<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/09/03/shedd-aquarium-beluga" target="_blank" > rescued beluga whales died</a> at Shedd Aquarium, the institution said it is closely monitoring the remaining whales and expressed concern that others may have health concerns after examination. </p><p>In a statement Friday, Shedd indicated that while many of the mammals are showing more "encouraging health signs than others," several belugas have "presented clinical concerns and their health can change quickly."</p><p>"None are yet where we want them to be from a health standpoint," the statement said. "We remain unwavering in our commitment to their care. When we agreed to rescue these animals from the threat of euthanasia, we knew there would be challenges and that they would require intensive, individualized care and close monitoring as they adjusted to this significant transition."</p><p>The report comes after a 20-year-old female named Rain, recently rescued from a shuttered Canadian aquatic park, and 34-year-old Beethoven died on Wednesday of unclear causes. </p><p>The deaths occurred about a week after another rescued beluga, Peekachu, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/26/one-of-the-shedds-rescued-beluga-whales-has-died" target="_blank" >also died of unknown causes</a> on Aug. 25. </p><p>Shedd is part of a consortium of four U.S. and one Spanish aquarium that together agreed to take 30 belugas languishing in Marineland, located in Niagara Falls, Canada. Marineland had faced criticism for years that its animals were living in unsanitary conditions.</p><p>The park closed to the public in 2024, and Marineland officials, citing extreme financial difficulties, had threatened to euthanize the whales if permanent homes couldn’t be found.</p><p>Shedd received 10 Marineland belugas, more than doubling their resident population.</p> <p>The aquarium said the belugas' condition can change daily and even hourly, and Shedd staff will adjust care based on individual needs, including diet and hydration requirements, which are being monitored. </p><p>Jim Robinett, who spent 40 years working at Shedd, including overseeing all marine mammals, said it’s unlikely that the deaths are the result of something contagious among the mammals.</p><p>“I’m sure they’ve already addressed that,” Robinett said. “When they receive new animals, generally there is a physical done at the sending facility and then when we receive them, we would do follow-up work as well.” </p><p>That follow-up would include blood work, checking the animal’s breathing and overall body condition, he said.</p><p>“Going forward, despite the loss of the three animals, they are probably not changing things in a major way. The obvious question is: Is there something in common with these three whales [that died]?”</p><p>One thing in common: They were all relatively old in whale years. </p><p>Whales in captivity rarely live to be 30 or older, Robinett said. Rain, at 20, was the youngest of the three that have died. </p><p>Beethoven was the oldest — 34; that’s “ancient” in whale years, Robinett said.</p><p>“The fact that they all may have all died from old age is probably a longshot, but these are not young animals. And despite our very, very best efforts, there is always some stress involved with the movement of an animal,” Robinett said.</p><p>Robinett said he’s certain that Shedd staff are talking to veterinarians at the four other facilities that received Marineland Canada belugas: Georgia Aquarium, SeaWorld San Antonio, SeaWorld San Diego and Oceanogràfic València in Spain.</p><p>“That’s exactly what they are doing. Are you guys experiencing similar conditions? Is there anything with your whales that we should be aware of? It’s a great network of veterinarians and they communicate all the time,” Robinett said.</p><p>The Sun-Times has reached out to all of the other receiving aquariums and heard back from Georgia Aquarium. </p><p>In a statement, the aquarium said they are “grieving with Shedd during this unimaginable time,” while also adding, “Georgia Aquarium received two male beluga whales, Balor and Zephyr, as part of the international rescue out of Marineland of Canada. Balor and Zephyr are settling in nicely with our existing beluga whale pod, discovering their new surroundings, and interacting with trainers.”</p><p>This is not the first time a Marineland beluga has died after being flown to a U.S. aquarium. Five belugas were transported to Mystic Aquarium in Connecticut from the Canadian aquatic park in May 2021. </p><p>Three <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/beluga-whale-deaths-mystic-aquarium-settlement-67041316b8b1af33a37f5f38774577dc" target="_blank" ><u>later died</u></a>, including one just three months after arriving at Mystic, according to the Associated Press. All three belugas died from illnesses attributed to genetic health problems, Mystic Aquarium officials said at the time.</p>

entries.title: What have we learned from the just-finished Brewers-Cubs series?
entries.summary: <p>The week that was for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> was one that can be used as a foretell into the realities they may (will?) face if a deep or even respectable (anything but a repeat of last year) postseason run is in the cards they play solitaire with.</p><p>With the series they just completed against the Brewers being both faith and fortune. Exposing everything we knew, wanted to know, didn’t want to know and may have been better off never finding out.</p><p><b>Game 1:</b> A yard-leaving explosion of sounds of nine inches of white, stitched leather leaving 2.61 inches of barreled wood. A Wrigley symphony, Concerto 9. Blue euphoria. 17-3. As one fan, drunk but coherent, said to someone an hour after the game who asked about the game, ‘‘If this was Ali-Frazier, they would have stopped it early.’’</p><p><b>Game 2:</b> A crowd pop of Brewers fans made enough noise for ESPN’s Jeff Passan to think Wrigley North had, for a moment, turned into American Family Field South. No sweep. No problem. Just as long as the Cubs send the Brewers a message in this series. The Brewers welcomed the Cubs to September, when baseball begins to matter more. 9-4, the score. Still the kings of the Central. Fact, not folklore.</p><p><b>Game 3:</b> The ceremonial return of the guy who had his official coming-out party at the Cubs’ expense in the 2025 postseason. Specifically, Game 5. It’s as if Jacob Misiorowski’s whole 2026 season has been a carryover from that. Until this game. Until the third inning. Where after five runs the Cubs ghosted the plate like Joe Jonas did Taylor Swift, circa 2008. Only one hit against the Brewers’ pen. A Dolly Parton win for Milwaukee. Forever and always runs through Milwaukee’s veins. Sweat trickles from underneath everyone’s Cubs cap. Even Craig Counsell’s.</p><p><b>Game 4:</b> ‘‘Why are Brewers so much better than the Cubs?’’ was the title of the first email I saw when I woke up Thursday. Their season’s version Ali-Frazier IV on Addison in wait. The buzz entering Wrigley far from defeated. Fans from Murphy’s to the Cubby Bear: We got this. Postseason-series energy. The pitchers’ duel Paul Skenes (Pirates) and Logan Webb (Giants) were supposed to have earlier in the week took place between the Wintrust and Budweiser scoreboards. W’s flew. Hubris resurfaced. Leaving Wrigley? Relief was what the North Siders soaked their minds-at-ease in, 16-ounce cups at a time.</p><p><b>The Day After:</b> The difference between artful and artificial is slowly disappearing. But to Cubs fans, not fast enough. The results they were looking for coming into the Brewers series left them still searching. They know their team is legit. A series like this at this time of year showed it. But against the Brewers, are they a legit threat? As in, one game better in a series? As in, one game better the next two times they face each other again?</p><p><b>The Aftermath:</b> ‘‘Playoff-caliber’’ is a term that has been tossed around in relation to the Cubs for the last two seasons. At this point, it’s no longer a compliment. The latest episode — not the last, as the play, rinse, repeat part of the season against the Brewers comes to its three-game finale in the coming week — has the chance to repurpose some of what wasn’t gained in this zero-sum standoff between the two. Even as the coming week in Milwaukee may not have the same meaning, there is room for the Cubs going into the postseason replacing that ‘‘caliber’’ with ‘‘contender.’’ Flipping what has become a<br>indictment back to a compliment.</p><p>Recaps aside, set aside that the Brewers retained a eight-game lead on the Cubs after the fact. Against the Brewers, if this altruism we choose to suffer with is to stay at 1,000%, here is what the Cubs are up against: a team that has won at least 86 games in the last nine full seasons, a team that entered play Friday with 73 wins when it scores at least four runs, a team that entered play Friday 75-3 when it goes to the ninth inning with a lead.</p><p>The Brewers’ ‘‘stats don’t lie’’ weakness? They only win 31% of their games when being outhit by their opponents. The problem with that for the North Siders in blue is that while they are tied for third in the league in hits and sixth in batting average, the Brewers are third in average and second in hits. Damn.</p><p>If anything, the Cubs were able to prove they have the ability to disprove the ‘‘Nobody beats the Miz’’ theme that the Brewers have been hanging over every team’s consciousness during the season. But the Brewers’ other pitchers? Way, way, way underrated.</p><p>The Cubs’ electability right now remains socialistically conservative. The noise has been there and continues to get louder surrounding them. Finally, it seems as if the promise of the Cubs is catching up. The proverbial (universal?) goal of the season was 90 wins. That means nothing now. If, say, they win 17 of their final 20 games but lose the upcoming series against the Brewers, all else becomes superficial.</p><p>Which, when you do the math, makes the end of this regular season very simple in games left to play: Now it’s down to three.</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Will the offseason be extension season for White Sox, Munetaka Murakami and Will Venable?
entries.summary: <p>First baseman Munetaka Murakami and manager Will Venable are two of the key figures in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ surprisingly winning season.</p><p>Murakami injected life into an anonymous and sputtering franchise, hitting tape-measure home runs and giving the Sox a truly international star. Venable, in his second season as manager, has been credited with nurturing young players and creating an atmosphere conducive to success.</p><p>General manager Chris Getz would like both to stick around past next year.</p><p>After his free-agent market collapsed, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/12/21/white-sox-to-sign-japanese-slugger-munetaka-murakami" >Murakami signed a two-year, $34 million contract</a> in December. In hindsight, the deal looks like a bargain for the Sox, even though Murakami hasn’t hit a home run since Aug. 18 and went 3 for 24 and struck out 12 times on the recent seven-game road trip.</p><p>Getz said Friday that the Sox and Murakami’s camp will “continue to have those conversations” about extending the relationship. Clearly, all parts of the Sox franchise are hoping he re-signs, even if it’s hard to see Murakami not getting a substantial raise.</p><p>On the field, when he’s right he’s one of baseball’s most powerful left-handed bats who knows how to work a count. Off the field, the Sox have benefited from his presence by marketing him extensively and perhaps gaining new fans in Japan.</p><p>“He’s been part of the success that we’ve had this year. It’s helped us win games,” Getz said. “It’s helped others gain confidence up here and belief that you can win games. That’s certainly something that we’re grateful for and thankful that we’ve gotten the opportunity to get to know him further. He’s a tremendous teammate, hard worker and he’s been productive.”</p><p>Just not as productive recently. Murakami is trying not to press through the slump, which has come at a bad time for the Sox, trying to hold off the Guardians for an AL Central title.</p><p>“Just keeping the same routine, the same preparation each day, each game. Very important to continue that,” Murakami told reporters Thursday in Houston via an interpreter. “And once that comes along, it’s going to be a different road again. That’s where I’m trying to go.”</p><p>The Sox know they’d like to go into their future with Venable, whose contract terms were never confirmed, but the franchise has traditionally given managers three-year deals. If that’s the case, Venable would enter 2027 on the last year of his contract if he’s not extended.</p><p>Hired Oct. 31, 2024, Venable walked into one of the toughest spots possible for a first-time manager. The Sox had just lost 121 games after being managed by the overmatched Pedro Grifol and well-meaning Grady Sizemore. The team didn’t need some changes, but a complete demolition and rebuild.</p><p>In just two years, Venable and the Sox are in first place with under a month left. Clearly, Venable hasn’t been perfect: the August gaffe when his second first-inning mound visit forced the Sox to remove Noah Schultz was a demerit, and his game management and bullpen moves have been questioned.</p><p>On Friday afternoon, Getz was full of praise for Venable, saying he’s been “fantastic” and done what the Sox have wanted and beyond. The Sox GM said he “definitely” wants Venable to be part of what they’re building, but added that they’re too focused on winning games to talk contract, and isn’t concerned about that topic because of the duo's relationship.</p><p>“He’s been a great partner to me. He’s been a great teammate to the coaching staff and the players,” Getz said. “So, he’s definitely a guy of high value to us and want to continue to find ways to nurture that relationship.”</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.summary: <h2>Moon Alert</h2> <p>Avoid shopping (except food and gas) and important decisions from 3:30 a.m. to 10 a.m. After that, the moon moves from Gemini into Cancer.</p><h2>Aries (March 21-April 19)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> Today you're more sensitive about home and family and might feel hurt if someone makes a disparaging remark. Conversations might be confusing. Someone might make an assumption. Don't agree to anything important today. entries.title: Providence's young stars sparkle in shutout of Joliet Catholic
entries.summary: <p>Providence's Brayden McKay and Isaac Patton checked off a couple career milestones on Friday night, and they did it in emphatic fashion.</p><p>McKay took the opening kickoff 92 yards down the right sideline for his first kick return touchdown, and Patton had a 96-yard interception return for his first pick-six as the No. 5 Celtics earned a dominant 27-0 home win against Will County rival Joliet Catholic.</p><p>Broden Mackert broke off a 69-yard touchdown run and Dominic Vita threw a 22-yard TD pass to Jaden Malone for Providence (3-0), which beat JCA for the first time since 2023.</p><p>The Celtics are winning with some of the best young impact players in the area. McKay, Patton and Vita all are juniors, while Malone is a sophomore. Of the players contributing to the scoring, only Mackert is a senior.</p><p>McKay was the secondary returner last season behind Xavier Coleman, who's now playing at Western Illinois.</p><p>"This year was my opportunity," McKay said. "Last game they didn't kick me the ball. Game before that, they weren't ready to kick me the ball either. So they finally kicked me the ball [and] I had to show what I can do.'</p><p>The quick score was just what the Celtics needed, Patton said.</p><p>"The whole sideline got hyped," he said. "The bleachers got hyped as well. Everybody was hyped for the kid."</p><p>As they were for Patton late in the first half. Down 14-0, Joliet Catholic (1-2) got.big defensive play of its own when Dylan Travis picked off a Providence pass and returned it to the Celtics' 22.</p><p>But Patton flipped the momentum two plays later with his 96-yard pick-six. He saw the receiver he was covering go out, saw another Hilltopper coming and jumped the route for the intercepetion. Then it was a foot race.</p><p>"Read the blocks, took it to the end zone," he said.</p><p>In the second minute of the third quarter, Mackert broke off his big run en route to a 12-carry, 109-yard night. Vita threw for 101 yards on 9-of-14 passing with one interception.</p><p>Mackert's TD made it 27-0 and was more than enough offense against Joliet Catholic, which was held to 107 total yards.</p><p>"The big thing is just every time they get a chance to make a play, they take advantage of it," Providence coach Tyler Plantz said of his players. "A couple of those guys made some great picks and then every single kid — I mean, testament to the 10 other guys that are out there throwing blocks for their teammates. ... That's the coolest thing."</p><p>Plantz appreciates the Celtics' selflessness.</p><p>"It's never, 'Look at all the yards I had, how many touches I had,'" he said. "It's, 'How did we all work together?' And [we're] starting to build that identity of a team that plays together, whether it be blocking on a kickoff, a punt.</p><p>"Doing all the little things that we're starting to figure out as a program has been really, really awesome."<br></p>

entries.title: No stars, no problem: Lincoln-Way East hands Homewood-Flossmoor first loss of season
entries.summary: <p>Lincoln-Way East is a giant of Illinois high school football. Coach Rob Zvonar has built one of the elite programs in the state during the last 25 years. Recently, the Griffins have featured some of the most talented players in school history.</p><p>But that isn’t the case this season. Zvonar jokingly refers to his team as ‘‘the kids that were left over at the playground.’’</p><p>Lincoln-Way East surprised everyone with a victory against Brother Rice in Week 1. Then the Griffins went to Kankakee and won in Week 2.</p><p>There was another test <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/03/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" target="_blank" >Friday</a> in Flossmoor. The host Vikings hadn’t allowed a point in the first two games of the season.</p><p>But No. 3 Lincoln-Way East took care of business again, knocking off No. 10 Homewood-Flossmoor 38-7 with a dominant all-around performance.</p><p>‘‘Personally, I don’t think there should have been lower expectations,’’ Griffins junior linebacker Ryan Manzke said. ‘‘We came out and beat Brother Rice because this team is a brotherhood. That is how we did it.’’</p><p>Manzke grabbed an interception and returned it eight yards for a touchdown in the third quarter to put Lincoln-Way East ahead 31-0.</p><p>‘‘I was staying in my zone,’’ Manzke said. ‘‘Hands went up. Ball went up. Bang! I was right there for the touchdown.’’</p><p>It was a humid, steamy night, and the slick ball and sweaty bodies led to multiple fumbles by both teams and more than a dozen instances of helmets popping off.</p><p>But nothing fazed the Griffins (3-0).</p><p>‘‘They really enjoy playing hard-nosed football on Friday nights,’’ Zvonar said. ‘‘They came out here and kind of controlled the game from start to finish . . . so that was impressive.’’</p><p>Lincoln-Way East senior Aidan Cavanaugh had 20 carries for 45 yards and a touchdown. Quarterback Evan LeFevour was 9-for-20 for 122 yards with one interception. He connected with Landon Martinez on an 18-yard touchdown pass in the second quarter.</p><p>‘‘We have been working our butts off since January,’’ Griffins junior Ryan Harris said. ‘‘We kept our heads down and didn’t listen to anyone else. We knew what we could do.’’</p><p>Many successful high school programs across the state reload each year and win without college-bound players and big-name stars. But that is much harder to do in Class 8A.</p><p>‘‘This has been very rewarding,’’ Zvonar said. ‘‘I wasn’t sure it was going to go this way in Week 1. And I wasn’t sure how it was going to go tonight. A little bit of the success is culture and tradition.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">It is all Lincoln-Way East so far. Evan LeFevour to Landon Martinez for an 18-yard TD. <br><br>Griffins lead Homewood-Flossmoor 14-0 in the 2Q. <a href="https://t.co/nWqFDvJLGS">pic.twitter.com/nWqFDvJLGS</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2096043446167363836?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Vikings (2-1) scored on a nine-yard touchdown pass from junior quarterback Karter Nicholson to Xavier Pratt in the fourth quarter.</p><p>‘‘Our defense has been playing pretty well, but our offense and our special teams put our defense in some really bad spots tonight,’’ H-F coach Troy McAllister said. ‘‘We were stout at times early. But when it is short fields, a team like East is going to get points.’’</p><p>The Vikings opened the season unranked, then took down highly regarded Bolingbrook 31-0 in Week 1 and Richards 35-0 in Week 2.</p><p>‘‘We had a couple of nice wins, but when you watch the film, you don’t feel great,’’ McAllister said. ‘‘We knew we were going to have moments this season with the ebbs and flows of high school football. Who we are right now is an inconsistent team.’’</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-140000" name="html-embed-module-140000"></a><blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports/video/7681902173231303966" data-video-id="7681902173231303966" style="max-width: 605px;min-width: 325px;" > <section> <a target="_blank" title="@michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports?refer=embed">@michaelsobriensports</a> Ryan Manzke breaks down Lincoln-Way East’s big win against Homewood-Flossmoor. <a title="ihsa" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/ihsa?refer=embed">#ihsa</a> <a title="football" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/football?refer=embed">#football</a> <a title="lincolnwayeast" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/lincolnwayeast?refer=embed">#lincolnwayeast</a> <a target="_blank" title="♬ original sound - michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/music/original-sound-7681902257894607646?refer=embed">♬ original sound - michaelsobriensports</a> </section> </blockquote> <script async src="https://www.tiktok.com/embed.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Son feels shunned by father over physical appearance
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 62-year-old man. I was born with a cleft lip and cleft palate. Growing up, I had several surgeries and much dental work to improve my appearance. I had wonderful friends who never teased me about it.</p><p>Now, looking back at my childhood, I realize that my father hated me because of the way I looked when I was born. He has never asked me to spend time with him and was always angry with me. Even now, when he sees me, I can feel the hatred he has toward me. I really hate being around him, but I sometimes have to see him at family gatherings. How should I handle this? — <i>ANGRY AND CONFUSED</i></p><p><b>DEAR ANGRY AND CONFUSED:</b> Start by remembering to cherish your wonderful friends and consider yourself lucky to have so little contact with dear old Dad. Handle family functions by limiting your direct interaction with him. Be cordial, but maintain a comfortable distance. Focus on the rest of the family and enjoy their company. Many families have members who don't get along, but it doesn't have to cause drama.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> Several weeks ago, I got a phone call from a stranger. She asked if I was the "Steve Hall" who had been in the Marines, and whom she remembered from high school. I told her I was not, and that I grew up in a different part of the country. Then I got a letter from her, asking essentially the same thing. She called again, and I repeated my answer and wished her luck.</p><p>I'm writing because I am concerned for her. She appears obsessive or perhaps very forgetful. She seems able to use the internet and make phone calls, she is calm and polite, her letters are brief and lucid, and she has neat handwriting. Like I said, though, her persistence seems odd. I'm just a little concerned. What would you do in this situation? — <i>STEWING STRANGER</i></p><p><b>DEAR STRANGER:</b> This interaction has all the signs of a scam. You have already allowed this person to identify you as someone who answers calls from unknown numbers. If you mentioned the letter to her, you have verified the physical address that goes with your phone number.</p><p>Be aware that the caller herself may not perpetrate the scam. She may be merely a scout who identifies possible victims for the real scammers. In the future, block all calls from unknown numbers. Also be wary of mail from unexpected sources. Do not respond to any offer that seems too good to be true or to anyone demanding payments that don't make sense to you.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am approaching 80 and am healthy and fairly active. When I look in the mirror, I see a pleasant-looking old woman, but when photos are taken at holidays, I look even older than I am — and scary — like the granny in the old Addams Family comics. What do you suppose is wrong with these modern cameras? — <i>BETTER THAN THAT IN ATLANTA</i></p><p><b>DEAR BETTER THAN THAT:</b> The problem is they are taking photos in high definition. However, this problem is easily solved. You can ask the photographer to touch up the photos electronically to make everyone appear flawless, or you can wear sunglasses while viewing them.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Employee-owned businesses do a good job protecting, uplifting workers
entries.summary: <p>The call went out over the company radios: Man down.</p><p>Everyone looked stricken. I raced to the part of the campus where my colleague was on the floor, in cardiac arrest, turning blue.</p><p>I knelt down on the floor, sweating, and began to perform CPR. For three minutes, I pushed and breathed into my co-worker. </p><p>At the end of my turn, two nurses and another member of the response team at my work, S&C Electric Company, took over. Together we got him breathing on his own before the paramedics arrived and rushed him to the hospital. Now I see him at work every day.</p><p>You don’t know how you’ll react during an emergency, but my emergency response team training at S&C Electric Co. paid off.</p><p>Rogers Park-based S&C is employee-owned through an employee stock ownership plan — a federally regulated retirement plan that allows companies to share ownership with workers. Because we're employee-owned, everyone takes pride in safety.</p><p>Companies with such a plan have up to <a class="Link" href="https://smlr.rutgers.edu/sites/default/files/Documents/Centers/Institute_Employee_Ownership/ResearchBriefs/January2024_RB_ESOPs_Workplace_Safety.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_blank" >13%</a> fewer workplace safety incidents than companies that don't, and workplace injuries and illnesses decline significantly within two years of a company implementing an employee stock ownership plan. Researchers attribute the improved safety at the companies to reduced employee turnover and increased employee involvement in managerial decision-making. There's alignment between what the employer and the employees want.</p><p>This Labor Day I'm sharing my story with the goal of increasing employee ownership for other American workers. My hope is that more workers can share the pride I have at work. There are just <a class="Link" href="https://www.nceo.org/research/employee-ownership-by-the-numbers" target="_blank" >301 </a>employee stock ownership plan companies in Illinois. Employee owners across the country are uniting to change that through <a class="Link" href="https://expandingesops.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Expanding ESOPs</u></a>, a coalition of nearly 100 organizations.</p><p>Employee ownership helps create a workplace where people are trained to look out for one another — something every worker deserves.</p><p><i>Marquis Spivey, lead electrical technologist, S&C Electric Co.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0a0000" name="module-0a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Showcasing West Side’s potential with Fifth City spirit</h3><p>The Sun-Times’ Abby Miller's recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/28/woodlawn-central-apostolic-church-hub-black-life-south-side-groundbreaking" >story on Woodlawn Central</a> is worth celebrating. A development centering Black culture, housing, businesses, jobs and community space represents the kind of investment our neighborhoods deserve.</p><p>It also raises the question: Where else in our city has this vision already been imagined, and what would it mean to invest there with the same ambition?</p><p>The West Side-based <a class="Link" href="https://www.3arts.org/projects/fifth-city/" target="_blank" >Fifth City</a> movement began over 60 years ago as a collaboration between neighborhood residents and the Ecumenical Institute. Its premise was both simple and radical: Communities could shape their own futures through comprehensive, resident-driven development. Fifth City understood that "revitalization" alone could not address housing, economic opportunity, culture or community spirit. They had to move together, with residents of all ages participating in the work.</p><p>That history matters now.</p><p>This is not a call to pit the West Side against the South Side or to diminish the promise of Woodlawn Central. It is a call to recognize that Chicago already has a powerful blueprint for community-led transformation in Fifth City — one that deserves renewed attention, investment and imagination.</p><p>That work is not only historical. Artists, residents and cultural organizations are still invoking <a class="Link" href="https://fifthcityrevisited.net/About" target="_blank" >Fifth City</a> today. This fall, the creative collaborative <a class="Link" href="https://www.honeypotperformance.org/" target="_blank" >Honey Pot Performance</a> will gather West Siders through <a class="Link" href="https://givebutter.com/pleasure_power_portal" target="_blank" >“Pleasure Power Portal,”</a> a month-long series rooted in memory, pleasure, Black cultural life and collective belonging at First Church of the Brethren and other West Side spaces. In 2027, Honey Pot Performance proposes to develop a new, original multidisciplinary performance, "Fifth City: Then and Now," which examines the future of the West Side and imagines what equitable futures could look like when legacy residents are centered as the authors — not just witnesses — of neighborhood change.</p><p>Remembering Fifth City should be more than an act of preservation. It should be an invitation to funders, developers, civic leaders and neighbors to revisit what this community built and ask what it could become again with sustained investment.</p><p>Woodlawn Central shows what is possible when Black community life is treated as infrastructure worth building around. Fifth City deserves that same recognition, and the resources to carry its vision forward.</p><p><i>Honey Pot Performance Core Team:</i> <i>Kimeco Roberson, Meida McNeal, Aisha Jean-Baptiste, Jo de Presser, and Jennifer Ligaya</i></p><h3>Bolster CPS, park district after-school activities </h3><p>As a retired Chicago Public Schools educator, Chicago Park District employee and the district's director of athletics and activities, I believe there would be less violence if the youth had access to recreational and social activities, including athletics and other activities kids are interested in. The research tells us if children participate in organized activities, they perform better academically, attend school more frequently and have fewer discipline referrals and higher graduation rates.</p><p>Everyone cannot make school sports teams, but if funding is added for social and recreational clubs and activities, all children can have an opportunity to participate in after-school activities at their schools with peers. The park district should also be offering free recreational athletic programs along with homework rooms, game rooms, animation club, woodshop, drama club and sewing and music classes. These programs should run from 3 p.m. until 10 p.m. weekdays with instructors and time slots for each age group.</p><p>CPS and the park district are undervalued and underutilized. Free programming is a great weapon that not only combats violence but helps teach life skills that will produce well-rounded young people and eventually well-rounded adults. </p><p>I've heard Mayor Brandon Johnson talk about the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/mayor/press_room/press_releases/2024/april/2025-myc-applications.html " target="_blank" >Youth Commission</a> that advises the city on key policies and initiatives. Experienced professional experts who can design effective fall, winter and spring programs should also be included in these discussions. </p><p>CPS and park district programs can be the change agent to address some civil disobedience and help to shape young people. I would love to serve.</p><p><i>Calvin Davis, Beverly</i> </p><h3>Cellphoning it in </h3><p>Being rabidly tradition-bound, I never owned a cellphone until now. I admit, at 73, I now see cellphones' portability, compactness, ease of use and game-changer versatility. </p><p>I bought in mainly for security on late-night walks. Such serenity didn't exist generations ago; you just risked facing an emergency without a pay phone nearby. Good luck finding an operable one today. To tap the cellphone's unprecedented assurance level, in contrast, you only need to be toting it.</p><p>I love texting too, messaging people I'd rather not talk to. It’s also nice to engage on Facebook and catch the music and live sports events on YouTube. I check the time, weather and consult Wikipedia and Merriam-Webster. And what an inspired leap for originators to mix in a camera!</p><p>Doubtless, camera manufacturers weren't enthused, nor Walgreens, in losing film sales and developing business. But innovations can spur others and further progress, like my processing incoming checks by photographing and depositing them via phone and bank app.</p><p>Our world certainly remains anxiety-ridden. But it continues to offer consolations, including my companion in the breakproof case, which I’ve already dropped many times like everyone else, only starting at a much older age.</p><p><i>Tom Gregg, Niles</i> </p><h3>Deep dive </h3><p>President Donald Trump thought small when he renamed<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/27/trump-signs-order-renaming-lake-ontario-as-lake-america-in-the-united-states" > Lake Ontario “Lake America.”</a> He also thought small by renaming the Gulf of Mexico the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/02/11/gulf-of-america-on-google-maps-united-states-users" >“Gulf of America.” </a></p><p>Trump needs to get on with renaming every body of water after his family and friends. I will be more than happy to help him there. Let’s rename Lake Erie to "Lake Vance." "Lake Musk" would be an excellent choice for renaming Lake Superior. "Lake Rubio" would be a great name in lieu of Lake Michigan. Trump can rename Lake Huron to "Lake Mullin" to honor of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin</p><p>Let's not forget the oceans. The "Melania Ocean" would be a wonderful choice for the Pacific Ocean. Renaming the Atlantic Ocean to the "Barron Ocean" is an obvious choice. The Indian Ocean can be renamed the "Frederick Ocean" in honor of Trump's father. </p><p>I don't know why Trump didn't think "bigly." </p><p><i>Shane Nodurft, Old Irving Park</i></p><h3>Apple and Google’s gaffe </h3><p>Shame on <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/08/30/politics/google-maps-changes-lake-ontario-to-lake-america" target="_blank" >Google</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/apple-maps-changes-name-lake-ontario-lake-america-rcna595667" target="_blank" >Apple</a> for changing the names of the Gulf of Mexico and now Lake Ontario on their maps for no other reason than to appease a petulant whiner of a president. </p><p><i>John Farrell, DeKalb</i></p><h3>Republicans got what they voted for</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://time.com/article/2026/09/01/white-house-east-wing-ballroom-trump-supreme-court/" target="_blank" >Four hundred million dollars</a> of our money going to pay for a gaudy ballroom. <a class="Link" href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cn8kz80n157o" target="_blank" >Hundreds of millions</a> of our dollars to upgrade a plane that was given to Donald Trump as a foreign gift. Millions of our dollars to an inept contractor to resurface the reflecting pool, which ultimately failed. Paying <a class="Link" href="https://steady.substack.com/p/wheres-the-beef" target="_blank" >24% more</a> for beef since Donald Trump took office. Paying at <a class="Link" href="https://www.notus.org/economy/gas-prices-trump-areas-republican" target="_blank" >least 40% more</a> at the pump to fill up your vehicle. The Republicans in Congress are evidently all OK with this. If you are OK with this, by all means vote Republican. But don't come crying when it gets worse.</p><p><i>Thomas Bajorek, Burbank</i> </p><h3>Shaking my head </h3><p>Keeping up with the unprecedented insanity of the Trump administration is exhausting. There's geographic name changes — first the Gulf of America, and now Lake America. There were already inhumane immigration policies, and now there are electrified gloves to stun immigrants. What next? Donald Trump bobbleheads sold in vending machines in the Lincoln Memorial? I think one bobblehead in the White House is more than enough.</p><p><i>Sheryl Gallaher, Palos Park</i></p><h3>Grousing guest</h3><h3></h3><p>I saw that President Donald Trump is making plans to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/08/30/trump-chairman-western-suburbs-presidents-cup-golf-tournament-sports" >visit the Chicago area</a> later this month. After years of bad-mouthing the city and using it as a punching bag to extol about violence, it will be nice to finally see him show his face here.</p><p>Hopefully he will spend a few minutes to meet with some Chicago area residents and not just fly in to hobnob with the golfers.</p><p><i>Steven Fortuna, Naperville</i></p><h3>Social Security solution?</h3><p>For as long as I can remember we were told Social Security will run out of money. Likewise, I could never understand why there was a salary cap on which Social Security taxes were calculated. Why not tax all wages? Why should the wealthiest among us receive a tax break? </p><p>My solution is to exempt the first $100,000 of salary from Social Security taxes and tax every dollar after that. Everyone gets a break, and it would greatly benefit the poorest among us. Now I don’t know the optimal amount to exempt, but I am sure someone can determine that, such that it benefits the poorest while making Social Security solvent for years to come.</p><p><i>Michael Sienkowski, Tinley Park</i></p><h3>Kiss off</h3><p>I was astonished to see the Sun-Times front page on Aug 31. I thought the National Tattler had arrived on my porch. How ridiculous and irresponsible to inflate the Lyons Township mini "scandal" with a front page kiss photo. I expect better from the Sun-Times.</p><p>Last Sunday morning, NASA launched the new <a class="Link" href="https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/" target="_blank" >Ruth Roman Space Telescope</a>. It's now on its million-mile voyage and will explore the universe for all mankind. That's front page news! The Sun-Times could have put that photo on the front page.</p><p><i>Blaise J. Arena, Des Plaines</i><br></p>

entries.title: Once the largest Methodist church in the Midwest is slated for demolition
entries.summary: <p>The long-vacant and decaying City Methodist Church — at one time the largest Methodist church in the Midwest — is slated for demolition, more than 50 years after it closed.</p><p>The wrecking ball comes after a number of unsuccessful attempts to save the historic church in Gary, Indiana. </p><p>In 2018, city officials worked with Chicago-based architecture firm Bailey Edward on a redevelopment plan for the site, which spurred the idea for an open-air ruins that made use of the church's structure.</p><p>Gary and the University of Notre Dame's Housing and Community Regeneration Initiative then came up with a vision in 2025 to use the church's bell tower for a proposed City Renaissance Park — part of a larger strategic plan to revive Downtown Gary. In January, the city’s redevelopment commission approved spending $112,500 to work with Bailey Edward on a plan for stabilizing the bell tower and cathedral so it could be incorporated into the new park. </p><p>But because a funding partner was never found for the $4.2 million stabilization effort Gary leaders decided to demolish the property, according to Steve Segura, chief communications officer for the city of Gary.</p><p>The Northwest Indiana Regional Development Authority solicited bids for the church’s demolition earlier this year. During its monthly board of directors meeting on Wednesday, the agency awarded the contract to Homrich Wrecking, who estimated demolition costs at $5.3 million. </p><div class="Enhancement" William G. Seaman founded City Methodist Church in 1926.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Demolition will begin after the contract is finalized, according to David Wellman, Northwest Indiana Regional Development Authority's communications director.</p><p>Segura said the church had been deemed unsafe and unrecoverable so Gary Mayor Eddie Melton needed to address the safety concerns after a funding partner was never found<b>.</b> The church, 577 Washington St., is located near the 21st Century Academy charter school and Genesis Towers, which opened as Hotel Gary in 1926 and converted into senior housing in the 70s.</p><p>“Ensuring the safety and well-being of our students and some of the community's most vulnerable residents in the immediate vicinity had to become the City's foremost responsibility,” Segura said in a statement.</p><h3>Steel roots</h3><p>Immigrants and migrants came to Gary in the 1900s, as the city boomed with steel mills. </p><p>As the population swelled, Rev. William G. Seaman founded the church in 1926, according to the Indiana Historical Bureau. U.S. Steel helped fund the church’s construction with $350,000, equivalent to about $6 million in 2026.</p><p>The church was open everyday and was a central meeting place in Gary. It included a gym, theater, music studio, cafeteria and commercial space. The congregation was segregated, though it offered programs to Black residents and immigrants.</p><p>When the city saw an influx of Black residents and immigrants in the 1950s, some City Methodist leaders tried to integrate the church. But its white congregation largely opposed the move, according to the bureau. And by the 1960s — when Gary's white residents fled to the suburbs — the church's population started to shrink. Efforts to build relationships with the community came too late. </p><p>"City Church leaders considered merging with a local Black church, but when community interviews revealed that minority groups did not trust the church, leaders decided to close in 1975," according to the <a class="Link" href="https://blog.history.in.gov/city-church-spirituality-and-segregation-in-gary/" target="_blank" >bureau</a>.</p><p>Lauren Pacheco, artist and board member of Landmark Illinois, said the church has been “taken by the elements” over the years, but the building is still striking<b> </b>with its intricate limestone work and terra cotta detailing.</p><p>“It's hard not to look at the building and get sort of drawn into a story of what history might have been like, or what life would have been like walking the halls in that building,” Pacheco said. “The Gothic Revival architecture and the sheer scale of it reflected what enormous confidence and ambition the city of Gary [had] at that moment. In that moment, it wasn't just a sanctuary. Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She said the church's demolition should be treated as a “significant moment” to think about Gary's future.</p><p>It's not the only property slated for demolition. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/09/08/city-gary-genesis-convention-center-wendall-campbell" target="_blank" >Genesis Convention Center</a>, which played host to Whitney Houston and Prince, will be torn down and the site redeveloped. This follows the demolition of other historic properties like the Gary Water Tower and Gary Memorial Auditorium in 2020. </p><p>Pacheco, who has lived in Gary for nine years, hopes city officials consider saving materials from City Methodist for a sculpture or similar display. The site could become a spot for open-air painting or photography, she said, since previous plans to create a ruins garden were dropped.</p><p>The city didn’t respond when asked if it was — or plans to be — in conversation with local groups about the future of the site. </p><p>Pacheco said it’s not always possible for every historical site to be saved. And in a city like Gary that has seen decades of economic decline, she argues it’s important to not become a museum of the past. If the City Methodist site becomes an</p><p>other hub for civic and community engagement, it could help contribute to Gary's progress.</p><p>“It could be a lovely way to engage residents to create a new sort of civic space — something that the City Methodist was celebrated for, “ Pacheco said. “This site, although taking a different shape, could mean something really special."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/powerless/2026/08/29/still-rebuilding-gary-celebrates-city-on-michael-jacksons-birthday" >Still rebuilding, Gary celebrates city on Michael Jackson’s birthday</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Assistant Photo Editor Pat Nabong. Follow her on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/patnabong" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3><b>What makes this photo important?</b></h3><p>South Chicago Chapel made headlines when 56 decomposing bodies were discovered in the funeral home in August. Since then, families have come forward with rage and doubts over how their loved ones' remains were handled. On Sunday, some families whose loved ones were cremated by South Chicago Chapel held a vigil outside the boarded-up establishment to demand answers about the contents of the urns that were given to them. At least two families say they believe that the urns they received may contain rocks, not their relatives' remains.</p><h3><b>How did you get this photo?</b></h3><p>Shawnese Shannon's family is among them. Her family, including her daughters Franquella and Marshawna Campbell, attended the vigil. Reporter Cindy Hernandez and I previously connected with the Campbells for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/28/sisters-mothers-cremated-remains-south-chicago-chapel-funeral-home" >a story that was published in the Sun-Times</a>.</p><p>During the vigil, the Campbell sisters set up an altar for Shannon in front of the boarded-up entrance of South Chicago Chapel. Some of Shannon's grandkids were lingering around the altar, and when I saw one of them crouch down, I framed the photo to highlight the looming exterior of the funeral home.</p><p><b>Technical entries.title: Baseball has eased America out of its slumps
entries.summary: <p>In 1856, baseball was anointed the <a class="Link" href=" https://www.loc.gov/exhibitions/baseball-americana/about-this-exhibition/origins-and-early-days/" target="_blank" >“national pastime”</a> in a letter to the editor in the New York Mercury newspaper.</p><p>On Feb. 2, 1876, Chicago businessman William Hulbert helped form the <a class="Link" href=" https://www.history.com/this-day-in-history/february-2/national-league-of-baseball-is-founded" target="_blank" >National League</a>, which included the Cubs — then called the White Stockings — as a charter member.</p><p>The game survived two world wars, racism, steroids, the infield fly rule, the designated hitter, George Steinbrenner and even the Black Sox scandal. It endured the Great Depression, <a class="Link" href="https://www.mlb.com/news/history-of-star-spangled-banner-national-anthem-in-mlb" target="_blank" >inspired </a>our national anthem to be payed at all sporting events and became a great American constant. </p><p>The game also saved America more than once, most memorably in recent history after Sept. 11, 2001, when America took a gut punch with New York City's twin towers crumbling to the ground and nearly 3,000 people losing their lives.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-280000" name="module-280000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>When the Atlanta Braves played the Mets at Shea Stadium 10 days later, it was the first professional sports game played in New York following the 9/11 tragedy. During the<a class="Link" href="https://www.nydailynews.com/2019/09/10/ex-mets-bobby-valentine-and-jay-payton-reflect-on-liza-minnellis-powerful-performance-of-new-york-new-york-at-shea-stadium-during-first-game-after-911/" target="_blank" > seventh-inning stretch</a>, Liza Minnelli inspired Americans with her emotionally rousing “New York, New York” performance before a packed house featuring many uniformed first responders. </p><p>Liza even stopped to hug and <a class="Link" href="https://www.nydailynews.com/2019/09/10/ex-mets-bobby-valentine-and-jay-payton-reflect-on-liza-minnellis-powerful-performance-of-new-york-new-york-at-shea-stadium-during-first-game-after-911/" target="_blank" >kiss</a> Mets center fielder Jay Payton, who was waiting on deck. </p><p>It was a first-rate example of what historian and philosopher Jacques Barzun meant when he <a class="Link" href="https://bleacherreport.com/articles/212819-when-baseballs-best-cultural-critic-turned-his-back-on-the-game" target="_blank" >said</a>, <i>"</i>Whoever wants to know the heart and mind of America had better learn baseball."</p><p>From Ernest Thayer’s poem <a class="Link" href="https://poets.org/poem/casey-bat" target="_blank" >“Casey at the Bat,”</a> Abbott and Costello's <a class="Link" href="https://www.baseball-almanac.com/humor4.shtml" target="_blank" >“Who’s on First?”</a> comedy bit and Lou Gehrig’s "Luckiest man on the face of the Earth" <a class="Link" href="https://baseballhall.org/discover-more/stories/baseball-history/lou-gehrig-luckiest-man" target="_blank" >speech</a>, baseball has energized America.</p><p>On Jan. 15, 1942, President Franklin D. Roosevelt issued his iconic <a class="Link" href="https://baseballhall.org/discover/baseball-history/baseball-digest-still-enthralling-fans-in-eighth-decade" target="_blank" >“green light” letter</a> to baseball Commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis. It was just 39 days after Pearl Harbor, and he was publicly encouraging the game of baseball to keep stirring America’s soul:</p><p>"I honestly feel that it would be best for the country to keep baseball going. There will be fewer people unemployed, and everybody will work longer hours and harder than ever before," Roosevelt said.</p><p>The American pastime, in fact, became a virtual participant in the World War II effort. More than <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2042550/2020/09/04/the-comeback-no-5-world-war-ii-vets-returning-home-to-star-in-the-majors/" target="_blank" >500 major league players</a> served in the Armed Forces, including 39 future Hall of Famers like Yogi Berra, Ted Williams, Joe DiMaggio and Hank Greenberg.</p><p>With more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.war.gov/Multimedia/Experience/Navy-Baseball/" target="_blank" >4,000 minor leaguers</a> joining them, the service branches were soon awash with baseball players. </p><p>During World War II, the <a class="Link" href="https://pugetsoundnavymuseum.org/navy-baseball-in-wwii/" target="_blank" >Great Lakes Naval Station</a> in North Chicago actively recruited solid players to dominate other service teams. It saw 43 Major League Baseball players join its ranks as it compiled a war years record of 188-32.</p><p>Baseball’s war impact went still further during this period. Many of the 130,000 American prisoners of war overseas were skilled baseball players and were commonly allowed to play ball in the <a class="Link" href="https://mcfarlandbooks.com/product/pow-baseball-in-world-war-ii/" target="_blank" >German camps</a>. The Germans didn’t mind the entertainment, plus the elevated morale made the days a bit easier for all. To be clear, these camps weren't picnics. Indeed, all of them were dreadful. But baseball sometimes brought a rare human moment to the darkness.</p><p>The game has always possessed a swashbuckling, gritty charm sometimes driven by colorful miscreants like Branch Rickey, Bill Veeck, Charlie Finley and Ted Turner. It also comes with the continual warts such as 2025's <a class="Link" href="https://www.espn.com/mlb/story/_/id/46917665/mlb-betting-guardians-clase-ortiz-pitch-rigging-indictments" target="_blank" >illegal pitch-rigging and sports betting indictments</a>.</p><p>Yet even baseball’s guile sometimes commands a certain allure. On April 29, 1983, the Cubs lost a close one to the Dodgers before a sparse Wrigley Field crowd while dropping to 5-14. When asked about growing fan criticism, frustrated manager <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/07/10/former-cubs-manager-lee-elia-rant-dies-les-grobstein-wrigley-field-phillies-dallas-green" >Lee Elia</a> uncorked an unforgettable three-minute rant spiced with 30 or so f-bombs as he supported his players but attacked the fans, saying, “Eighty-five percent of the world is working; the other 15 come out here.”</p><p>How can we reconcile baseball’s disparate personality and contradictions? We don’t. Perhaps that is the beauty and the allure driving the game’s genuine Americana. It is also why Liza performing at Shea not only worked, it was virtually inevitable. With that stirring televised moment, America was enabled to be itself once again.</p><p><i>Eldon Ham is a faculty member at IIT/Chicago-Kent College of Law, teaching sports law and justice. He is the author of five books on the role of sports history in America.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c80000" name="module-c80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>
