entries.title: What do you think of efforts to build data centers in Chicago? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked what readers think of efforts to build data centers in Chicago. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"We need to keep up with the rest of the world. If we don't build them, then we fall behind as a society and as a country."<br><i>— Drew Pekala</i></p><p>"Build them only in communities where the median home price is above $3 million. Make them build their own power source that is not connected to our public grid. Do not give them a single cent in tax breaks. Enact strict environmental protections for water usage, emissions and noise pollution."<br><i>— Austin Child</i></p><p>"How do we live in a time period where natural resources are becoming scarce, and people still think data centers are OK?"<br><i>— Sergio Antonio Cueto Tellez</i></p><p>"Great. If they make money, they should be paying their own way and then some. No corporate tax benefits, no discounts and no dumping."<br><i>— Christine Bock</i></p><p>"Our precious resources such as our Great Lakes are at serious risk of depletion and pollution. Electricity rates will continue to skyrocket with no caps or end in sight. They create noise, light, air and water pollution, ruin the environment, wetlands and kill wildlife and negatively impact property values. The list is long and very concerning."<br><i>— Deborah Bullwinkel</i></p><p>"They need to be built. There just needs to be a better methodology for where and how."<br><i>— David Mansfield</i></p><p>"If they can supply their own power up to regulatory spec, sure, why not. But they have to address infrastructural and environmental concerns. And taxpayers and ComEd customers better not see even a penny of cost."<br><i>— Adam Agosto</i></p><p>"It should not be done. Especially in heavily populated areas. Statistics are just now coming in about the adverse impact on wildlife, people, businesses, communities and natural resources."<br><i>— Alyce Langreder-Garcia</i></p><p>"Build something that will make life better for Chicagoans. There's a very long list of deferred maintenance on infrastructure, public services are being cut, etc. Data centers are not needed."<br><i>— Tim Patterson</i><br></p>

entries.title: Chicago’s highest-ranking cops must answer for subordinates’ misconduct
entries.summary: <p>Chicago needs police accountability that travels up the chain of command — not just downward.</p><p>Officers should be held accountable when they violate the law, department policy or the rights of the public. But accountability shouldn't necessarily end with the officer who breaks the rules or abuses his or her power.</p><p>Police departments are hierarchical organizations. Policies, priorities and expectations flow downward through command, supervisors and ultimately to officers.</p><p>Recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/20/chicago-police-cpd-copa-vecchio-snelling" >reports</a> about Joseph Vecchio, who racked up more complaints than any other Chicago police officer in recent years and was part of a unit with a pattern of conducting improper traffic stops, illustrate why responsibility and oversight should flow to the top.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ee0000" name="module-ee0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Complaints, lawsuits and disciplinary matters tied to traffic stops raise legitimate questions about supervision, training and performance expectations. </p><p>So what responsibility do those in the higher ranks bear when their subordinate is formally found to have engaged in misconduct?</p><p>When patterns of complaints or litigation emerge, were appropriate supervisors and commanders monitoring those patterns? Were officers receiving clear guidance about lawful and constitutional policing? Were performance expectations communicated in a way that encouraged sound police practices rather than simply producing numbers?</p><p>During my last position on the now defunct Community Safety Team, I raised concerns and filed complaints through appropriate channels about what I understood to be inappropriate and unethical mandated activity expectations involving questionable traffic stops.</p><p>Specifically, as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/police-reform/2025/10/16/chicago-police-cpd-franklin-paz-michael-barz-traffic-stop-misconduct-lawsuit-settlement" >reported</a> by WBEZ's<b><i> </i></b>Tom Schuba in 2025, I took issue with pressuring officers under my command to make at least 10 traffic stops each shift — an order I believed was an unlawful quota.</p><p>What followed was harassment and intimidation, including being dumped from the unit and sent to a midnight shift. Then retroactively, I was falsely accused of violating a police rule in an attempt to terminate me after I filed a formal complaint. Ultimately, I was forced to sue. The city settled shortly before trial, and I was subsequently cleared of wrongdoing.</p><p>I do not bring up this experience here to revisit the allegations, identify individual employees or disclose matters that may be confidential. Nor do I suggest that my experience establishes wrongdoing by anyone who was not found responsible through the appropriate process. </p><p>Rather, my experience reinforced a broader concern.</p><p>Officers are expected to exercise independent judgment, follow the law and comply with department policy. Those responsibilities are fundamental.</p><p>But officers also work within a command structure. They receive assignments, guidance, priorities and expectations from supervisors and commanders.</p><p>When significant expectations are communicated to officers, leadership should be able to explain what was expected, why it was expected and what safeguards were in place to ensure that the expectation was consistent with constitutional policing, department policy and sound police practices.</p><p>That is not an accusation. It is basic organizational accountability.</p><p>Chicago has invested heavily in police reform, oversight and accountability. Those efforts are important.</p><p>But meaningful accountability should not consist solely of identifying an individual officer after a complaint, lawsuit or disciplinary investigation occurs.</p><p>It should also examine the circumstances surrounding the conduct.</p><p>Were training and policy requirements being followed?</p><p>Were concerns raised by officers or members of the public appropriately evaluated?</p><p>And when oversight agencies identified potential problems, were those concerns taken seriously and addressed?</p><h3>Badge, rank doesn’t excuse misconduct</h3><p>The answers should be based on evidence — not rank, reputation or politics.</p><p>I am not suggesting supervisors should be blamed whenever an officer makes a mistake. Police work involves difficult decisions, and individual officers remain responsible for their own conduct.</p><p>But leadership also carries responsibility for establishing clear expectations, providing appropriate supervision and correcting problems when warning signs become apparent.</p><p>If one officer makes a mistake, investigate that officer.</p><p>If multiple officers operating within the same organizational environment encounter similar problems, there should be an examination of whether there are broader issues involving policy, training, supervision or management.</p><p>Accountability should not be a system in which rank-and-file officers bear the consequences of organizational decisions while the decisions and expectations that influenced their work receive little examination.</p><p>The badge does not excuse misconduct. Neither should rank.</p><p>Every member of a police organization has responsibilities. Those responsibilities may be different, but accountability should exist at every level.</p><p>Next time Chicagoans read about unlawful traffic stops, they should demand more than the name of the officer who made the stop. </p><p>They should also ask: What expectations surrounded that stop, where did those expectations originate and what oversight existed to ensure they were lawful, constitutional and consistent with department policy?</p><p>Those inquiries should be answered through evidence, transparency and a fair examination of the entire chain of command.</p><p>Because when accountability travels only downward, the system is incomplete.</p><p>Responsibility must travel both ways.</p><p><i>Lt. Franklin Paz Jr. is a former supervisor of the Chicago Police Department’s now defunct Community Safety Team.</i> </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bc0000" name="module-bc0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><hr><p></p>

entries.title: Bears RB D'Andre Swift somehow 'finding another gear,' sees fast start coming for rushing attack
entries.summary: <p>Here’s a great place to start for any running back: The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ D’Andre Swift got the work he needed in training camp but didn’t play a snap in a preseason game and is fully healthy heading toward the season opener.</p><p>‘‘Hell, yeah,’’ Swift said last week.</p><p>He made that celebratory comment a few days before exiting late in the Bears’ final preseason practice Thursday, but a source said that was merely cramping and that there’s no concern about him going into the regular-season opener Sept. 13 at the Panthers.</p><p>That’s good for the Bears because they’re going to need him.</p><p>Quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/01/money-isnt-everything-with-a-big-contract-in-reach-qb-caleb-williams-wants-to-make-sure-bears-keep-winning" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a>’ pass plays go viral, but the ground game is the foundation of the Bears’ offense. It’s at the heart of coach Ben Johnson’s creativity and precision, and nobody on the roster runs like Swift.</p><p>He always has had elite speed and elusiveness, but he reminded everyone last season about how tough he is running between the tackles, even at 5-8 and 204 pounds. The Bears can count on him getting at least a couple of yards, and that can become a breakaway in a blink.</p><p>And, somehow, he seems faster than ever. He probably isn’t, not at 27, but it sure looks that way. Maybe he’s just processing plays more rapidly.</p><p>‘‘Going into the second year in this system, I have a better understanding of the offense in general and where I need to be,’’ Swift told the Sun-Times. ‘‘I feel really good about it.</p><p>‘‘It’s the first time I’ve been in a system for consecutive years in a while, so I paid attention to the self-scout from last year and figured out what I need to do a better job of. I’m honing in on the little details, so that allows me to play faster.’’</p><p>That has been evident all summer.</p><p>Swift drove the Bengals crazy in their joint practice a couple of weeks ago, leaving them shouting expletives in his wake. New running backs coach Eric Studesville, who replaced Eric Bieniemy, sees a decisive runner. And right guard Jonah Jackson’s most logical assumption, based on what he has seen in practice, is that continuity has helped Swift recognize everything more quickly when he has the ball.</p><p>‘‘He’s always been a pretty polished runner,’’ Jackson said. ‘‘But he seems to be finding another gear.’’</p><p>Swift was better across the board last season than he was in his first with the Bears. His yards per carry spiked from 3.8 to 4.9, and he finished with 1,087 yards (12th in the NFL) and nine touchdown runs (11th).</p><p>He helped the Bears finish third in rushing, which was an incredible turnaround from 25th the season before and invaluable amid the inconsistency in their passing attack.</p><p>‘‘There’s no reason we shouldn’t get off to a fast start,’’ Swift said of the ground game this season.</p><p>Johnson has said he wants to get Swift more involved as a receiver after he had 34 catches for 299 yards and a touchdown last season. That lone touchdown catch illustrated what makes him a rare weapon for Williams. He caught a pass just past the line of scrimmage against the Commanders and took it 55 yards to the end zone. It’s the type of no-risk, high-reward proposition every quarterback loves.</p><p>The Bears ideally would balance the workload between Swift and Kyle Monangai — Swift got 223 carries last season to Monangai’s 169 — but Johnson has said Monangai’s timetable to return from a knee injury he suffered in practice Aug. 16 is ‘‘week-to-week,’’ so it might be all Swift in the opener.</p><p>The history between Johnson and Swift dates to 2020, when Johnson was a low-level Lions assistant and the team drafted Swift in the second round. Johnson was the Lions’ offensive coordinator three years later, when they drafted Jahmyr Gibbs and traded Swift to the Eagles.</p><p>Neither seems stuck on their split. They’ve done nothing but rave about each other since reuniting. Johnson calls Swift a smart, explosive runner, and Swift describes Johnson as a genius.</p><p>At his best, Swift not only is a threat on his own but also a way of unlocking other aspects of Johnson’s offense. The better he runs, the more potent play-action becomes. And when Johnson goes to formations with three tight ends — something he did quite a bit last season and probably will do more this season — Swift’s presence in the backfield adds to the unpredictability.</p><p>That said, there’s a good chance this will be their last season together. Swift is coming to the end of his three-year, $24 million contract — now a bargain, given that he ranks 19th at his position in average annual pay — and it’s unlikely the Bears will shell out market value for him in a contract extension rather than look for a younger, more affordable option in the draft or lean on Monangai next season.</p><p>General manager Ryan Poles said the Bears ‘‘will look at’’ an extension for Swift and conceded he looks ‘‘amazing,’’ but he also noted it’s ‘‘tough . . . trying to figure out how you want to allocate everything’’ as the Bears look to budget for upcoming extensions for Williams and others.</p><p>‘‘But I love ‘Swifty,’ ’’ Poles said. ‘‘I love the way that he’s working.’’</p><p>They all do. And if this is his last run with the Bears, he’s poised to make it a big one.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: The anatomy of Barack Obama’s tan suit
entries.summary: <p>If you have former President Barack Obama’s famous tan suit, Jay Greenfield can confirm it’s the real thing.</p><p>“It could easily be identified,” he told me.</p><p>He and his brother Tod run Martin Greenfield Clothiers in Brooklyn, New York. They are the sons of Martin Greenfield, a Holocaust survivor who sewed his first stitches while a prisoner in Auschwitz, who went on to make custom suits for Obama, other presidents and an array of political figures, as well as famous actors and athletes.</p><p>“Everything we put in the suit is natural,” Greenfield said.</p><p>The Greenfield tan suit is a presidential artifact — the physical reminder from Obama’s eight years in the White House when the habitually dark suit-clad president wore a tan suit to an Aug. 28, 2014, press conference. That tan suit drew the wrath of Obama’s right-wing critics. Reporters were told this summer he gave it away years ago after cleaning out a closet.</p><p>The suit originally had a hand-cross-stitched Martin Greenfield label inside the jacket. The tailors also placed a small printed label in a jacket pocket with Obama’s name, date and the order number. However, I’m told by former Obama staffers a label with Obama’s name was most likely removed before the suit was given away. I’m still hunting for the place where it was donated.</p><p>Here’s the anatomy of the custom Obama suit:</p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-cc79d942-a89f-11f1-ae40-5d8f50155072"><li>It’s called the “Martin Greenfield Classic,” a traditional two-button suit with a notched lapel 3 ¼ inches wide. The jacket has flap pockets and side vents.<br></li><li>The suit is lightweight. It is made of a soft fabric called faille. “It’s a cloth that really holds its shape well and has a really nice appearance to it,” Greenfield said.<br></li><li>The suit has a 100% Bemberg lining. The brand’s fibers are derived from cotton. “That’s used in fine men’s clothing because it’s natural fiber, it’s breathable and it has a very nice feel to it, as opposed to anything synthetic,” Greenfield said.<br></li><li><p>The buttons are made of an opaque tan shade of water buffalo horn. “The ideal buttons for a suit,” Greenfield said.</p><p>The material is “super lightweight. It doesn’t really break when you press it, so it’s very lasting. Each button looks unique.” As a commercial clothier, Greenfield said they need to get permits to import the buttons.<br></p></li><li>The jacket is not heavily padded. The soft shoulders are made in layers, so “when you move your arms in a hand-tailored suit, the sleeve actually moves a little bit and the shoulder pads adapt to the person,” Greenfield said. “That is the art of tailoring in a quality custom suit.” <br></li><li>The buttonholes on the sleeve are hand-stitched and can be buttoned and unbuttoned. They match the lapel and front buttonholes.<br></li><li>Red, white and blue hand-stitching appears in the lining. “It takes a person sewing those stitches by hand, to have, like, three separate needles and going: one hand stitch with the red, one hand stitch with the white, one hand stitch with the blue,” Greenfield said.</li></ul><p><b><i>Contact us</i></b><i>: Please join us on this journey by sending tips, story ideas or suggestions on who to interview. Email: tansuit@suntimes.com.</i></p>

entries.title: New serial killer exhibition in Chicago offers rare artifacts from John Wayne Gacy, H.H. Holmes
entries.summary: <p>For 30 years, Karen Conti kept the three paintings John Wayne Gacy gave her facedown in her closet.</p><p>“What can you do with them? I can't display them. I'm not selling them because I would hate to profit. I just didn’t know what to do with them,” said the Berwyn native and lawyer who was part of Gacy’s legal team in his final death row appeals before being executed in 1994.</p><p>For the first time, that artwork will be on public display at the new “Serial Killer: The Exhibition” experience opening Saturday at Cinespace Chicago Film Studios.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>John Wayne Gacy gave his lawyer Karen Conti this canvas that portrays a pensive seaside with cresting waves and a low-hanging moon. He included a short description. “He said it was mysterious, just like he is,” she said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of K. Conti</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p> One piece is a skull clown that Conti calls “gross.” Another is a depiction of Gacy in the Pogo the Clown costume he wore to kid's parties and charity events that she deems “horrible.” But it’s the third painting that’s wholly unique from the garish characters Gacy typically focused on. It’s a canvas that portrays a pensive seaside with cresting waves and a low-hanging moon. Gacy gifted it to Conti for her birthday with a short description. “He said it was mysterious, just like he is.” </p><p>The rare art is some of the roughly 2,100 artifacts that appear across 40 detailed exhibition rooms. All together, the experience encompasses 21,000 square feet, housed in a building at the studio lot where shows like “Chicago P.D.” are filmed.</p><p>But inside here are real artifacts you won’t get in scripted shows or the latest made-for-streaming true crime series. There’s Jeffrey Dahmer’s jailhouse Bible and signature glasses, the pair of LA Gear high-top sneakers Aileen Wuornos wore when she was arrested in 1991 and a scrap of a trash bag that Ted Bundy used in his assault kits. Not to mention there are copious court documents and letters, realistic recreations of crime scenes like Ed Gein’s lair, a virtual reality simulation room and a 20-question game toward the end to determine where you fall on the psychopathic pendulum. </p><p>Special attention is also paid to local killers like Gacy and “Devil in the White City” murderer H.H. Holmes as well as less famous ones like Richard Speck, Lester Harrison, Robin Gecht and Tillie Klimek.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b50000" name="module-b50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Serial Killer: The Exhibition</h3><br><b>When:</b> Opens Sept. 5<br><b>Where:</b> Cinespace Chicago Film Studios, 2428 W. 15th St. (parking is available at 2406 W. 15th St.)<br><b>Tickets:</b> $38+<br><b>Info:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://serialkillerexhibit.com/chicago/" target="_blank" >serialkillerexhibit.com/chicago</a></div> </div><p>It’s estimated that the whole experience will take 90-120 minutes to go through and it’s recommended for ages 14 and older (those under 14 must be accompanied by an adult). Still, many of the crime scene recreations are overly graphic so you may want to take that into consideration before bringing the family.</p><p>“I hope that guests see the educational part of this, the historical journey of what happened in the past to today so we can learn from it,” said Giancarlo Guerra, a representative with Italian exhibition creator Italmostre. The company has been bringing the experience to cities around the world for the past 10 years, with 2026 marking the U.S. debut. It’s expected to stay in Chicago through the end of January.</p><p> True to Guerra’s statement, the exhibition has artifacts from before the term “serial killer” was even coined (which happened in the 1920s), like ephemera from Belle Gunness, aka Hell's Belle, who tortured and murdered at least 14 men in Illinois and Indiana between 1884 and 1908. There’s also photos and hunting gear of the “newest” serial killer, Rex Heuermann, who was convicted in June of the Gilgo Beach killings. </p><p>“We wanted to make sure everyone is represented here,” Guerra added. For him, that also meant the victims. Many of the 150 killers profiled are featured alongside pictures, names and ages of the people whose lives were taken. In Gacy’s case, that includes the five unidentified boys and men that continue to be investigated by the office of Cook County Sheriff Tom Dart, according to Conti.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ec0000" name="image-ec0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c605271/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2Fec%2F3ccc0df047e4a39e655023804e6f%2Fserial-killer-the-exhibit-10-photo-courtesy-italmostre-copy.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0d090b7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2Fec%2F3ccc0df047e4a39e655023804e6f%2Fserial-killer-the-exhibit-10-photo-courtesy-italmostre-copy.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/87eb01b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2Fec%2F3ccc0df047e4a39e655023804e6f%2Fserial-killer-the-exhibit-10-photo-courtesy-italmostre-copy.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Serial Killer - The Exhibit (10) photo courtesy Italmostre copy.jpg" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/87eb01b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2Fec%2F3ccc0df047e4a39e655023804e6f%2Fserial-killer-the-exhibit-10-photo-courtesy-italmostre-copy.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/cf959c7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2Fec%2F3ccc0df047e4a39e655023804e6f%2Fserial-killer-the-exhibit-10-photo-courtesy-italmostre-copy.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/87eb01b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F94%2Fec%2F3ccc0df047e4a39e655023804e6f%2Fserial-killer-the-exhibit-10-photo-courtesy-italmostre-copy.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Serial Killer: The Exhibition” opens Saturday and runs through early next year at Cinespace Chicago Film Studios in North Lawndale.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Italmostre</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>By the final room of the exhibition, it concludes with a memorial wall listing all the names of the victims and a message that reads, in part, “For far too long, their names have remained in the shadows while the names of their killers became known around the world. This memorial seeks to restore what should never have been taken from them: their names, their memory and their dignity.” </p><p>For Dr. Bill Kimberlin, who donated nearly 400 items from his collection to the exhibit, victimology is a crucial part of his work as a clinical psychologist and professor at North Central State College in Ohio. He regularly corresponds with inmates like David Berkowitz and Scott Peterson who are currently serving life sentences. Kimberlin has also witnessed executions and sat in on last meals.</p><p>“Some have started confessing or providing more information to me and so my focus has been on bringing some closure to families. Because there's victims out there that haven't been identified yet and maybe [events like these] can help us investigate that even closer.”</p><p>As for why people have become so obsessed with true crime and events like “Serial Killer: The Exhibition,” Kimberlin has his theories, too. “I think our human nature is we want solutions and we want answers to everything,” he said. “And I think with so much content out there, it can be educational if done right. If you can see how forensics works, how psychology works, how the criminal justice system works and how it’s changed with technological advancements, I think that’s evident here.”</p>

entries.title: The remarkable story of the Holocaust survivor who made Barack Obama’s tan suit
entries.summary: <p>The story behind former President Barack Obama’s missing tan suit starts with Maxmilian Grünfeld, who was 15 when he arrived at the Auschwitz Nazi death camp by cattle car with his mother, father, two sisters, brother and grandparents in the spring of 1944.</p><p>He was the only member of his family to survive the Holocaust.</p><p>He later came to the United States, changed his name to Martin Greenfield and became a famous tailor in Brooklyn, New York.</p><p>He made Obama’s tan suit.</p><p>Greenfield’s first sewing lesson was in the concentration camp.</p><p>I’ve been on the hunt for Obama’s tan suit. When he wore it to a press conference on Aug. 28, 2014, instead of his usual dark suits, right-wing critics deemed it unpresidential. The overblown response to the suit worn by the nation’s first Black president sparked a political and cultural flashpoint. It is not at the museum in the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park, which opened June 19. Reporters were told Obama gave the suit away years ago, after cleaning out his closet.</p><p>I want to tell you about the remarkable life of the man who made it.</p><p>Much of the story I am telling you comes from <a class="Link" href="https://www.regnery.com/9781684515080/measure-of-a-man/" target="_blank" >Greenfield’s memoir</a>, “Measure of a Man, From Auschwitz Survivor to Presidents’ Tailor,” and from Jay and Tod Greenfield, his sons who now run the business.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Zubaer Khan/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>On Aug. 9, 1928, Greenfield was born in Pavlovo, a village in what was then Czechoslovakia, near the Hungarian border. It was the home to some 50 Jewish families. The town is now in western Ukraine.</p><p>Upon arrival at Auschwitz, Greenfield’s family faced Josef Mengele, the Nazi physician known for his horrific medical experiments. Mengele selected which prisoners would become slave labor and which would be sent directly to the gas chambers.</p><p>Greenfield and his father and a sister went into the slave labor line; the other family members went to their deaths. With men and women separated, Greenfield never saw his sister again. He last saw his father Joseph on their second day at Auschwitz.</p><p>Greenfield’s first job at Auschwitz was in the laundry, washing Nazi uniforms. He scrubbed the collar of an SS soldier’s shirt so hard it ripped. Greenfield wrote that the angry soldier “beat me until I bled.” The soldier threw away the torn shirt, but Greenfield kept it.</p><p>Another prisoner in the laundry knew how to sew. “He gave me a needle and thread and taught me how to sew a simple stitch,” Greenfield wrote.</p><p>He wore the Nazi’s mended shirt under his prison uniform. He believed he was treated better by the Nazis and other Jewish prisoners because the shirt seemed to convey a special status. He tore the shirt of another Nazi so he could have two.</p><p>“Of course, receiving your first tailoring lesson inside a Nazi concentration camp was hardly the ideal apprenticeship. I would have much preferred to hone my craft on [London’s] Savile Row or in the mills of Milan,” Greenfield wrote. “Looking back, though, that moment in the camps marked the beginning of the rest of my life. Strangely enough, two ripped Nazi shirts helped this Jew build America’s most famous and successful custom-suit company.”</p><p>The Nazis moved Greenfield and other prisoners from Auschwitz on Jan. 27, 1945. He endured a winter death march and train transport to arrive at the Buchenwald concentration camp on Feb. 5, 1945.</p><p>On April 11, 1945, American tanks arrived and Buchenwald became the first camp U.S. troops liberated.</p><p>The next day, Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower, the Supreme Allied Commander in Europe during World War II, toured the “human ruins” there. Greenfield wrote that Eisenhower was “ten feet tall in my mind.”</p><p>A few years later, Greenfield would find himself making suits for President Eisenhower.</p><p>But I’m getting ahead of the story.</p><p>The war was over. Greenfield learned his father also ended up in Buchenwald, but the Germans shot him about a week before the liberation.</p><p>Greenfield was living in a displaced persons camp in Germany when his mothers’ siblings in Baltimore and The Bronx, New York, tracked him down. On Sept. 11, 1947, the 19-year-old boarded the SS Ernie Pyle in Bremerhaven, Germany, and arrived in New York Harbor on Sept. 18, 1947.</p><h3>Greenfield, Obama and the Chicago tan suit connection</h3><p>At first, Greenfield lived in Baltimore, where he worked in an upholstery factory. He was reluctant to talk about the Shoah — the Hebrew word for the Holocaust — because he didn’t think a person raised in America would believe him. Eventually, he moved to New York and got a job as a “floor boy” at GGG Clothiers. He added English to the Czech, Hungarian, German and Yiddish he already knew.</p><p>Greenfield learned all the jobs related to the hand-tailored menswear business. He got to know some of GGG’s celebrity clients on the East Coast and Hollywood. He eventually became a GGG executive and oversaw the production of suits for Eisenhower, continuing to make suits for him into his presidency.</p><p>Thirty years after arriving in America, Greenfield bought the GGG factory in 1977 and renamed it Martin Greenfield Clothiers. It’s still in the same spot. The business has endured as other manufacturers in New York failed, Jay Greenfield told me. It is a union shop.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-1b0000" name="image-1b0000"></a> His first assignment was to make a set of white tie and tails for Clinton’s appearance at a Gridiron Club dinner with the Washington journalists in the club performing musical skits. Greenfield eventually made more than 20 suits for the 42nd president.</p><p>He recalled in his book that his relationship with Obama started in October 2010 “with an email Jay received from the legendary Chicago fashion retailer Ikram Goldman, owner of the Ikram boutique,” now at 15 E. Huron St.</p><p>“A style advisor to first lady Michelle Obama, Ikram had been asked to recommend an American tailor who could make fine suits for President Obama. She graciously recommended us,” Greenfield wrote.</p><p>Before Obama evolved toward custom menswear, some of his suits were from a storied Illinois company, Hart Schaffner Marx, founded in 1887 in Chicago.</p><p>At first, the Obama White House wanted to send suits for Greenfield to copy. Greenfield, through his son Jay, sent word that he did not copy suits made by others.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ec0000" name="module-ec0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Pursuit of the Suit</h3><br>On Aug. 28, 2014, the tan suit that then-President Barack Obama wore to a White House press conference became an unexpected story. After his presidency, Obama reportedly gave the suit away cleaning out his closet. Follow as former Sun-Times Washington Bureau Chief <b>Lynn Sweet</b> hunts down the original tan suit — and what makes it so compelling along the way. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/tansuit" target="_blank" >suntimes.com/tansuit</a><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-dddea0e2-a259-11f1-9f97-593067e43792"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/17/hunt-for-barack-obamas-tan-suit-help-us-find-it" target="_blank" ><b>We’re on the hunt for Barack Obama’s tan suit. Jay said they were told “no special pricing because he’s the president.” They were instructed to charge “the full retail price,” which then was about $2,000.</p><div class="Enhancement" interview that Obama told him he needed “summer campaign suits.” Obama pulled a suit out of his closet, a tan suit. He liked the color. It was, Jay recalled, “not quite beige, not quite khaki.” The Greenfields tried to match the color.</p><p>They made a few other suits “that were a bit lighter.” In all, Jay — who went to the White House eight times for fittings — estimates Obama ordered more than 15 suits over the eight years of his presidency, but only one tan.</p><p>Tod Greenfield checked the records and found the tan suit was in the works in March 2012. Obama wore it on June 16, 2012, when he attended the wedding of Valerie Jarrett’s daughter Laura. Jarrett, a longtime friend of Barack and Michelle Obama who served as a top adviser during his two terms as president, is now CEO of the Obama Foundation. She is also the person who told reporters in June that Obama gave away the suit cleaning out his closet. “We thought about a replica, but that would not be authentic,” she said.</p><p>Obama wore the tan again to Easter services on April 20, 2014, and a few months later at that press conference.</p><p>In 2012, the tan suit was made with pleated pants.</p><p>By February 2014, on Jay’s sixth White House visit, Greenfield recalls in his book, “[T]hey encountered a new influence on presidential fashion — the first daughters Malia and Sasha. ‘My girls tease me about my suit pants. … They say my pleats make me look old and uncool.’”</p><p>And so, in 2014, Greenfield made flat front pants for the suit so Obama could have two styles to choose from. Jay told me they were able to match the jacket because the mill was still making that fabric. made suits for a who’s who of clients: President Gerald Ford, then-Vice President Joe Biden, former Secretary of State Colin Powell and a slew of stars in movies and TV shows. Greenfield’s shop provided clothes for the “Boardwalk Empire” cast for all five years of the HBO series. The client list also includes Rat Pack singers Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and Sammy Davis Jr., comedians Jerry Lewis and Eddie Cantor, news anchor Walter Cronkite, basketball star LeBron James and film luminaries from Steve Buscemi and Jonah Hill to Denzel Washington, Leonardo DiCaprio, Paul Newman and Al Pacino.</p><p>If you think you picked up that tan suit in a secondhand store, it will be easy to verify it’s the real thing.</p><p>Greenfield, who died March 20, 2024, at the age of 95, added a special touch: There is distinctive red, white and blue hand-stitching in the lining.</p><p><b><i>Contact us</i></b><i>: Please join us on this journey by sending tips, story ideas or suggestions on who to interview. Email: </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:tansuit@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>tansuit@suntimes.com</i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: New Sox Park? Future owner announces proposal for riverside stadium at 'The Railyards'
entries.summary: <p>A new Chicago White Sox ballpark concept has been revealed amid the team’s push for a new stadium.</p><p>Canal Edge, a company owned by potential future White Sox owner Justin Ishbia, said the mixed-use development called The Railyards could be an option presented to the team as its lease at the publicly owned Rate Field ends.</p><p>The stadium would sit alongside the Chicago River stretching from Roosevelt Road to the north to 18th Street to the south, and bordered with the river on its east side and Canal Street to its west. The company has the land under contract.</p><p>The concept is in its “early stages” and is just beginning a monthslong study on the feasibility of transportation and environmental evaluations, the company said in a statement.</p><p>"The Railyards is about turning idle land into opportunity — for patients who need better access to care, for a team and its fans who deserve a dynamic Riverfront home, and for a city that needs jobs, housing, and economic investment," said Canal Edge controlling shareholder Justin Ishbia. "This is a Chicago project, built by and for Chicagoans, and we are excited about its potential.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/06/justin-ishbia-white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-ownership-winnetka" >Who is Justin Ishbia, the White Sox’ potential future majority owner?</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot in Chicago Lawn Friday night, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 28, was in an argument with another person in the 7300 block of South Kedzie Avenue at 11:15 p.m. when the other person shot him, police said. entries.title: Cubs' Shota Imanaga wants to ‘build trust back,’ Craig Counsell says story around lefty ‘a little incorrect’
entries.summary: <p>MIAMI – Friday was a good night for Shota Imanaga.</p><p>His six innings of one-run ball looked to be exactly what the Cubs needed from their lefty starter after back-to-back rougher performances.</p><p>Those outings – <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/23/cubs-mariners-brewers-nl-central-standings-shota-imanaga-stats-starting-rotation-playoffs" >a quick hook after two innings</a> two weekends ago against the Mariners and a loss to the Reds last weekend in which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/30/chicago-cubs-shota-imanaga-three-homers-cincinnati-reds-craig-counsell-jody-davis-jon-lester-ed-howard-edward-cabrera" >he allowed three homers</a> – couldn’t help but bring to mind Imanaga’s struggles down the stretch last season, when he had a 6.51 ERA and gave up 10 homers in five September starts.</p><p>“Building trust is kind of like dominos or Jenga,” Imanaga said through an interpreter Friday night, “where it takes time and it’s hard to build up, but in an instant it can disappear.</p><p>“I want to slowly build that trust back up and be that pitcher that everyone can trust.”</p><p>While frustrated fans have lamented Imanaga’s big home-run total – he didn’t allow any Friday but entered Saturday baseball’s co-leader with 33 surrendered – the Cubs have never vocalized any lack of confidence in the left-hander, and they saw Friday as the norm.</p><p>“I think maybe the story around Shota is a little incorrect,” manager Craig Counsell said Saturday. “We’re 7-2 in games he’s pitched since the All-Star break. He has an ERA [of 3.35] since the All-Star break.</p><p>“I think Shota sometimes is, frankly, held to a higher standard than everybody else. I’m not sure why. Guys give up runs. They give up runs. And maybe because of how it happens for Shota, it’s a little different?</p><p>“But Shota’s having a good season. He’s having a really good second half. And if you look at it in totality, that’s what it shows you.”</p><p>Though Imanaga’s season ERA is nearly 4.00, he could find himself with major league career highs in innings pitched and strikeouts.</p><p>A season has ups and downs for nearly all players, and Imanaga has been no exception. He had a terrific 2.32 ERA in his first nine starts this year before a particularly nasty stretch of four outings in which he allowed 26 runs and a dozen homers.</p><p>But that was followed by 10 great ones, during which he had a tiny 2.06 ERA. Then he had a 7.13 ERA in four starts. Then Friday night.</p><p>That lack of consistency is relative, of course, and more obvious and more troubling cases of whiplash are easy to find.</p><p>But it strikes as perhaps the sort of thing team president Jed Hoyer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/01/cubs-home-runs-record-jed-hoyer-front-office-pitching-starting-rotation-playoffs-postseason-shota-imanaga-matthew-boyd" >was talking about last week</a>, when he lauded the Cubs’ position-player group but cited the need for more consistent performances from the pitching staff.</p><p>Imanaga was more consistent last season before his September struggles, with a 3.24 ERA in a dozen starts after returning from the injured list, a number that was a wildly more impressive 0.91 if you remove his one seven-run clunker against the White Sox.</p><p>But then those troubles started, and by the time the playoffs rolled around, the issues he ran into in the regular season’s final month and the three homers he surrendered in a pair of postseason outings added up to the Cubs deciding against using him on regular rest in Game 5 of the NLDS, the final game of their season.</p><p>So might Friday’s bounce back mean a little more than just another round of ebbs and flows in Imanaga’s campaign?</p><p>“Any time you have consecutive starts that weren’t your best,” Counsell said, “you want the confidence and you want the feedback that says, ‘I got it.’</p><p>“And maybe the timing of the season is a little bit real for Shota, in terms of last year, he experienced a little downturn at the end of the season.</p><p>“From a confidence perspective, for Shota, it was important.”</p><p>Imanaga is just one piece of the Cubs’ starting-pitching puzzle, of course.</p><p>Trade-deadline additions Clay Holmes and Kevin Gausman have been excellent. And lefty Matthew Boyd has had a couple good outings in a row after a slight hiccup.</p><p>“We’re in good shape,” Counsell said. “We’ve got five guys we’re eager to give the ball to and comfortable giving the ball to. And they’re performing. We sit in a good spot, in terms of the rest of the regular season.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot in West Englewood early Saturday morning, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 29, was in the 6500 block of South Laflin Street at 2 a.m. when two people approached him and fired shots before fleeing northbound on the street in a blue sedan, police said. The man was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Morris quarterback Marion Persich's speed and size too much for Simeon
entries.summary: <p>Marion Persich’s transfer from LaSalle-Peru to Morris over the summer received a little bit of hype. The Warriors are always worth keeping an eye on, and Persich was seen as a player who could make a major difference in Morris. It has happened quickly.</p><p>The junior quarterback is listed as 6-4, 232 pounds, but the numbers don’t do his frame justice. Persich is thick, powerful and athletic. He broke free for an 81-yard touchdown run in the third quarter of the Warriors’ 44-27 win against visiting Simeon on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/03/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Saturday</a>, and the play showcased how difficult it is for defenses to contain his rare combination of size and speed.</p><p>A Simeon defender had a good angle for a tackle and met Persich ten yards from the end zone. Most high school players get smacked out of bounds or tied up and taken down at that point. Persich threw the defender to the ground, never breaking his stride.</p><p>“It was a read option and I saw the linebacker bail,” Persich said. “I was going to hit the defender, but I wanted the touchdown, so I put my arm out and hit him.”</p><p>Persich had 13 carries for 115 yards and two touchdowns. He was 8 of 12 passing for 128 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions.</p><p>“He’s a phenomenal athlete,” Morris coach Alan Thorson said. “Missed a few throws early on, but he adjusted. He’s a playmaker. There are little things that the crowd doesn’t see. He made some nice audibles today and changed some plays. Directional stuff where he saw openings in the defense.”</p><p>Persich threw a 35-yard touchdown to Quaid Phillips late in the first half to put the Warriors (3-0) ahead 31-7. He connected with Mick Smith for a 14-yard touchdown with 2:05 left to hold off a late comeback from Simeon (0-3).</p><p>“He is still not fully settled in, and he’s playing amazing,” Smith said. “He’s putting up good numbers and playing his tail off. Once we can put the little pieces of the puzzle together and get him comfortable, it is going to be fun.”</p><p>Morris opened the game with a quick-tempo drive that resulted in a three-yard touchdown run by Maxwell Skrtich. Then Simeon fumbled the kickoff, and the Warriors recovered. Persich punched in a one-yard TD run a minute later, and the Wolverines were down 14-0 before taking a snap on offense.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Simeon fumbles on the kickoff return. Morris recovers and this long pass from Marion Persich to Robert Kennedy sets up another TD. <br><br>Warriors lead 14-0 before Simeon takes a snap on offense. <a href="https://t.co/pMGGMdKr2G">pic.twitter.com/pMGGMdKr2G</a></p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2096301199662141668?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 5, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“Morris jumped on us fast,” Simeon coach Sinque Turner said. “You can’t play a team like this in a hole like that. I take some of the blame for what we were in during the first quarter. I knew they were a heavy-run team and we were playing a bit of zone, and that didn’t match. When we got into man coverage and sent some pressure, we were able to have our way here and there.”</p><p>Simeon cut the Morris lead to 38-27 on a 34-yard touchdown pass from sophomore quarterback Aki King to sophomore receiver Jalonny Billingsley with 5:18 left.</p><p>King was 13 of 23 passing for 370 yards with three touchdown passes, all to Billingsley, who finished with six catches for 194 yards.</p><p>“The guys persevered, and we played good football in the second half,” Turner said. “We don’t expect to get a bunch of calls coming all this way down south, but this is not on the refs. We have to get our act together. Morris is a perennial power, and we wanted to come down here and see it. We will get back to league play and do well. It is really about the state playoffs for us. This is to prepare.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-880000" name="html-embed-module-880000"></a><blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports/video/7682188014272990494" data-video-id="7682188014272990494" style="max-width: 605px;min-width: 325px;" > <section> <a target="_blank" title="@michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports?refer=embed">@michaelsobriensports</a> Marion Persich rushed for 115 yards and 2 TDs and threw for 128 yards and 2 TDs in Morris’s 44-27 win against Simeon. <a title="ihsa" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/ihsa?refer=embed">#ihsa</a> <a title="football" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/football?refer=embed">#football</a> <a title="morris" target="_blank" href="https://www.tiktok.com/tag/morris?refer=embed">#morris</a> <a target="_blank" title="♬ original sound michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/music/original-sound-michaelsobriensports-0?refer=embed">♬ original sound michaelsobriensports</a> </section> </blockquote> <script async src="https://www.tiktok.com/embed.js"></script> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: White Sox catcher Jake Rogers has experience — albeit unpleasant — in a division race with Guardians
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox just can’t shake the Guardians, and that’s a feeling catcher Jake Rogers knows all too well.</p><p>Rogers was with the Tigers last season when they blew a 10-game lead in the American League Central with 21 games left. At that point, it was the Royals chasing them. But soon enough, it was the Guardians, who went 19-4 down the stretch and won the division on the last day of the season.</p><p>On Sept. 10, the Guardians trailed the Tigers by 9 ½ games. On Sept. 23, the teams were tied.</p><p>“We’d be up six [runs] and be like, ‘Are we going to lose?’ ” Rogers told the Sun-Times. “It was a wild thing, and we still got in and ended up beating Cleveland. We got the one that mattered, I guess.”</p><p>Indeed, the Tigers beat the Guardians in the wild-card round, but Rogers’ tale is a cautionary one for the Sox, who took a 2 ½-game lead into their matchup Saturday with the Twins. That deficit is certainly more manageable for the Guardians, who won both games of a doubleheader Friday against the Tigers in walk-off fashion.</p><p>With them in the rearview mirror, no lead is safe — on the field and in the standings.</p><p>“You feel like they’re going to win every game,” Sox manager Will Venable said. “So if we just kind of put them to the side, put everyone else to the side, and focus on our stuff, that’s all that matters.</p><p>“But it’s hard not to be scoreboard-watching. Not just with Cleveland, but with everybody. It really is a distraction because we just want to take care of our business.”</p><p>The Sox also are monitoring the league standings, where they entered the day with a 1 ½- game lead on the Astros for the No. 2 seed in the AL playoffs and a free pass through the wild-card round. Losing three of four to the Astros last week in Houston was a blow.</p><p>Rogers’ experience last year could be invaluable for this young Sox team, and after Drew Romo was the one optioned to Triple-A Charlotte when Kyle Teel returned from injury Friday (though Romo is staying with the big-league club on the taxi squad because of his work with pitchers), Rogers is expected to see this playoff push to the end.</p><p>Among Rogers’ advice for teammates: All that matters is making the playoffs.</p><p>“Obviously, you want that bye, not a wild card,” he said. “The biggest thing once we made it in [last year], it was like, ‘Hey, look, all that matters is making it in.’ We’re playing for something right now. But you just want to be in because once you’re in, anything can happen. Playoff baseball is a different kind of game.”</p><p>Another piece of advice: Chase something.</p><p>“We’re being chased, and it’s happened where you kind of get lost in that,” he said. “The big thing is chase someone in front of you, whether that’s the Rays having the best record [in the AL]. Just try to chase something in front of you and be the steady players that you’ve always been and don’t try to do too much.”</p><p>Rogers has had quite an interesting season, his sixth in the majors. The Sox are his fourth team since July 30, when the Tigers traded him to the Orioles. The Orioles then traded him to the Red Sox, who waived him the next week. The White Sox claimed him Aug. 14, and here we are.</p><p>“It’s a great ballclub, truthfully,” he said. “It’s a young ballclub, and they all get along with each other. Camaraderie is a huge thing in this game. Been a part of some teams that didn’t have it and some teams that had it. I’ve enjoyed my time here, the few weeks that I’ve been here. It speaks volumes about this clubhouse just how easy it was to fit in.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Chicago Labor Day Parade and Eddie Fest highlights city's historic labor connections
entries.summary: <p>Chicagoans celebrated the city's ties to America's labor movements Saturday at the Chicago Labor Day Parade.</p><p>Organized and run by the Chicago Federation of Labor, the event has been held in the Pullman Historic District since 2023 to spotlight the community's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/11/15/revitalization-historic-pullman-aims-boost-tourism-country-first-company-town" target="_blank" >history and strong connection to labor</a>.</p><p>The parade was followed by Eddie Fest, named after United Steelworkers activist Edward "Oilcan" Sadlowski — an oiler and machinist at U.S. Steel South Works in Chicago who, at 25, became president of United Steelworkers Local 65 in the 1960s. Held in Steelworkers Park, it featured entertainment such as live music, community crafts and more.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Under pressure following drug arrest, Rosemont's Mark Stephens resigns as chairman of Triton College's board
entries.summary: <p>The embattled chairman of the Triton College board, Mark Stephens, has resigned his leadership post.</p><p>Stephens — who’s been under pressure to step down since a July 31 arrest on drug charges in far northwest suburban Harvard — is staying on the board as a regular member.</p><p>That’s according to a statement released Saturday by the taxpayer-supported school, which is based in River Grove and serves students from two dozen west and northwest suburbs, including Oak Park and Maywood.</p><p>“On September 4, 2026, Mark R. Stephens stepped down as Chairman of the Triton College Board of Trustees. Mr. Stephens remains a Trustee,” the statement from Triton’s press office says. “As Triton College’s Board of Trustees, we acknowledge Mr. Stephens' more than 30 years of service as Board Chair and recognize the dedication demonstrated throughout that tenure.</p><p>“To our campus and community, we remain committed to providing students with a supportive, high-quality educational experience, grounded in the institution’s mission of valuing the individual, educating and serving the community.”</p><p>The announcement came several days after a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/09/02/rosemont-mark-stephens-brother-brad-stephens-mayor-son-donald-stephens-triton-college-board-drug-arrest" target="_blank" >Chicago Sun-Times story </a>quoted two other elected Triton board members encouraging Stephens — a member of Rosemont’s ruling family — to leave the post.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </figure> </div> </div><p>One of those two members, Tracy Jennings, said Saturday that Stephens made the right decision but added: “That’s step one. We’ll see now how his case and all that goes.”</p><p>Stephens has an upcoming court hearing on his criminal charges. It’s unclear whether he can remain on the board if convicted.</p><p>When he was arrested during a traffic stop, police found cannabis and what was believed to be cocaine.</p><p>It's unclear who will become the next board chairperson, a position elected by all seven board members, but Jennings said he's interested in the job.</p><p>Stephens, 67, had been chairman since the early 1990s. A son of Rosemont's late founding Mayor Donald E.
